intro: In 2022 Mike wrote 122 public essays on memetics for marketers ([the full set](https://ambiguous-celery-039.notion.site/e4da53351c3442f18274588479d67b19?v=95abac9fd89e4b7da7aa5ba09711cfe0)). None of their claims was measured. Each row below is one claim, restated so that data could prove it wrong, with the cheap rival a neuron-based test would have to beat and the design or seed in [`IDEAS.md`](IDEAS.md) that tests it. Many of the claims do not need neurons at all: any consistent unit could test them, and the table says so. AI agents read the essays and wrote the rows; all ten chapters were read in full. Nothing here has been run.
sources_intro: The essays cite 994 sources, of which 96 are papers and 29 are books. These are the ones whose findings bear most on the programme. 'Not confirmed' means the agent could not check this session that the source exists under that title.

claims.claim: Batman, Zorro, the Scarlet Pimpernel and Iron Man differ in more surface details than they share, yet plainly belong to one family.
claims.hypothesis: Family members sit closer together when measured by active neurons than when measured by shared words, compared with matched heroes from outside the family.
claims.rival: TF-IDF (word counts weighted by rarity), sentence embeddings, an LLM asked which works belong together.

claims.claim: Stories descend from identifiable earlier stories: Pyramus and Thisbe to Romeo and Juliet to West Side Story, Hamlet to The Lion King, Die Hard to its many imitators.
claims.hypothesis: A family tree built from active neurons, on summaries with every name removed, recovers documented adaptation lines better than a tree built from words.
claims.rival: TF-IDF word overlap, sentence embeddings, and traits listed by an LLM that reads the text.

claims.claim: Many stories are an older story moved to a new setting: Zorro is Mexican Batman, Iron Man is Batman in California, The Lion King is Hamlet with lions.
claims.hypothesis: Take story A's neuron profile, subtract the neurons for its setting and add those for the new setting: the result lands close to story B's profile.
claims.rival: The same subtraction and addition done on sentence embeddings, which are known to handle analogies.

claims.claim: What audiences call original is a work whose sources they do not recognise, because the sources are obscure or the author forgot them.

essays.name: Where do you get your ideas?

claims.hypothesis: Works judged original sit just as close to their nearest earlier source as works judged derivative do; the source is simply less well known.
claims.rival: Nearest earlier sources found by sentence embedding, with fame taken from page views.

claims.claim: Only a small, fixed number of story shapes and chord sequences work on human brains: seven plots, six arcs, four chords.
claims.hypothesis: As more works are added to a collection, the number of distinct plot-level clusters stops growing.
claims.rival: Word-level methods already find such structure: the six-arcs study scored words for happiness. Embedding clusters are the other rival.

claims.claim: A famous idea cannot be copied while everyone remembers it, but a window opens once only the older generation recognises the source.
claims.hypothesis: Successful reuse of a bundle of memes follows a fall in how present the earlier work is in public attention.
claims.rival: Any unit will do, including plain remake records, combined with page views or word-frequency counts as the measure of attention.

claims.claim: Elements added by a later version can become a permanent part of the story, as the balcony scene did for Romeo and Juliet.
claims.hypothesis: The point where a new trait enters a line of descent can be dated, and the trait then persists in later versions.
claims.rival: Dating by the first appearance of a keyword, such as 'balcony'.

claims.claim: Fill-in-the-blank phrases (snowclones) such as 'the cure for the common X' or 'X made simple' keep spreading whatever fills the blank.

essays.name: The cure for the common meme

claims.hypothesis: Neurons for the frame fire regardless of the filler, including when the frame's own words are loosened.
claims.rival: A regular expression (a text pattern match), which wins on literal templates. Neurons only have a case on reworded variants, against embeddings.

claims.claim: Inventions appear in fiction before they are built, and inventors often credit the story.
claims.hypothesis: Memes for a device show up in fiction before they show up in patents or the press.
claims.rival: First appearance of the device's keywords. The neuron method adds little here; any unit can test it.

claims.claim: The Lindy effect: the longer a meme has already lasted, the longer it is likely to go on lasting.
claims.hypothesis: A meme's risk of disappearing falls as its age rises.
claims.rival: Any unit can test this (words, trope tags). The danger is that old memes are simply the common ones.

claims.claim: Film colour follows conventions that signal setting and genre: yellow for Mexico, teal and orange for action, set poster palettes by genre.
claims.hypothesis: Neurons in a vision model that respond to colour-grading conventions predict a film's genre and setting.
claims.rival: A plain colour histogram (a count of how much of each colour an image holds). Relevant to the image side experiment only.

claims.claim: Memes survive in bundles (memeplexes): each part loses its effect when another is missing, and none would be remembered alone.
claims.hypothesis: Sets of memes are passed on together across adaptations more often than chance allows, and removing one makes the rest less recognisable.
claims.rival: Words that tend to occur together; topic models (statistical groupings of words).

claims.claim: There is a best level of familiarity: too familiar and a message is ignored, too new and it confuses.
claims.hypothesis: Success rises and then falls (an inverted U) as a work's neuron-measured novelty relative to its category increases.
claims.rival: Novelty measured by keywords, genre tags or sentence embeddings.

claims.claim: The big idea (concept) of an ad matters most, the theme within it less, and small variants move results by only 1 to 2%.
claims.hypothesis: The further apart two ads are, the bigger the gap in their results; results vary more between concepts than between variants of one concept.
claims.rival: Human tags for concept, theme and variant; edit distance and embeddings as the distance measure.

claims.claim: Mixing memes from clashing sets (a country bar playing hip-hop) puts off both audiences.
claims.hypothesis: Texts that mix memes from bundles that do not normally go together are rated less appealing.
claims.rival: An LLM asked to rate how well the parts fit; human tags.

claims.claim: People still tag creative work better than machines, but language models will make tagging cheap enough to catalogue memes at scale.
claims.hypothesis: Tags from an LLM agree with trained human coders well enough to serve as the traits for family trees, and neuron readings add detail beyond those tags.
claims.rival: The LLM tags themselves. The claim is about LLM tagging against people; neurons enter only as a possible extra.

claims.claim: Each new medium (writing, print, broadcast, the internet) copies memes more accurately than the one before.
claims.hypothesis: The amount a text changes from one copy to the next falls after print arrives.
claims.rival: Change in wording alone (edit distance), which should show the effect without neurons. Data are hard to get.

claims.claim: A meme's spread follows an S-curve whose ceiling cannot be forecast until about 95% of the peak is reached; fringe communities show what goes mainstream next.
claims.hypothesis: Detecting a meme by neurons in fringe communities gives earlier warning of mainstream uptake than counting its keywords does.
claims.rival: Keyword and hashtag counts. The S-curve claim itself needs no neurons: curve fitting on counts can test it.

claims.claim: Over-used ideas wear out: a winning ad peaks at 4 to 6 weeks, and small variations of it only delay the decline.
claims.hypothesis: A new ad starts with weaker results when it shares memes with an ad the audience is already tired of.
claims.rival: Overlap in human-assigned tags. Mike's own evidence would need private ad data; public tests use headlines and reposts.

claims.claim: Rivals grow alike: competing brands copy whatever works for the other until their differences disappear.
claims.hypothesis: The distance between rival brands' copy, measured in neuron readings, shrinks over time.
claims.rival: Mike's own tag-count distance and TF-IDF word similarity, which will probably do as well because brands repeat their own words.

claims.claim: New ideas come in bursts from a few small places over short periods ("scenius", Brian Eno's word for the shared genius of a whole scene), not evenly from wherever people live.
claims.quote: the astonishing productivity of comparatively tiny geographic pockets of innovation
claims.hypothesis: Meme units that later spread widely first appear in a few place-and-decade cells far more often than each cell's share of all works predicts. Falsified if first appearances simply track where most works are made.
claims.rival: First uses of new words or phrases, dated and placed the same way. Any unit can test this; neurons add something only if they catch an idea before its words settle.
claims.data: Film plots with country and year (CMU Movie Summary Corpus, as in PO-23); papers with author city (OpenAlex). Film place data is by country only, which is coarse for a claim about cities.

claims.claim: Bursts of innovation follow the end of a catastrophe (war, plague, upheaval), because the crisis leaves a pool of people used to solving hard problems together. Decline then sets in until the next crisis.
claims.quote: Emergence from catastrophe is a theme common to most historical ‘Scenia’
claims.hypothesis: In the 10 to 20 years after a country's major crisis ends, its works introduce more first-appearing meme units per work than before, and more than matched countries with no crisis.
claims.rival: New words or new genre tags per work, counted the same way. No neurons needed. The essay's evidence is a handful of chosen cases, so crises followed by no burst are the real test.
claims.data: Film plots by country and year (CMU corpus, Wikidata) against dated ends of wars and crises; patents or papers by country as a second domain. Output volume and lost records confound it.

claims.claim: On remix platforms the version of a meme that goes viral is usually not the original but a later one that somebody improved.
claims.quote: Often it’s not the originator that goes viral with a new idea, it’s one of the many people who iterated on it
claims.hypothesis: In remix trees with declared parent links, the most popular item is a descendant more often than tree size alone predicts, and popularity rises with distance from the original over the first few generations.
claims.rival: None for the first part: declared links and view counts settle it. For what the winners changed, compare unit differences with word differences and with an LLM describing the edit.
claims.data: Platforms with declared parents and view counts, as in RX-S6 (Scratch, Thingiverse); TikTok sound and duet trees if they can be obtained.

claims.claim: Built-in remix tools, plus a feed that ranks every post on engagement, make memes change faster on TikTok than on any other network.
claims.quote: memes are mutating at a faster rate than is possible on any other social network
claims.hypothesis: The same meme tracked on two platforms gains more changes per copy and per day on the one with remix tools and an engagement-ranked feed than on a follower-feed platform.
claims.rival: Edit distance on captions and transcripts, hashtag variants, or an LLM describing what changed between versions. Any consistent measure of change will do; neurons matter only if words miss the change.
claims.data: Memes with dated instances on several platforms (Know Your Meme entries; public Reddit and Twitter samples). TikTok data access is the obstacle, and video needs transcripts first.

claims.claim: On a feed ranked by engagement, what is posted decides reach and follower count matters little. This reverses H28 (source beats content) for one kind of platform.
claims.quote: Even someone with millions of followers isn’t guaranteed distribution if what they post is bad.
claims.hypothesis: With the poster held fixed, content explains a larger share of a post's reach on engagement-ranked feeds than on follower feeds, and follower count explains a smaller share.
claims.rival: Follower count alone; sentence embeddings of the caption; an LLM rating the post. Neurons are needed only if they explain reach beyond these.
claims.data: The same creators posting the same items on two kinds of platform, with views and follower counts per post. CJ-S10 would need a second platform type added.

claims.claim: Every new advertising channel loses its response as it fills with ads, so marketers must keep changing messages just to stand still (a "Red Queen's race"). This is about the channel, not one idea as in H25.
claims.quote: The first online banner ads had a click through rate of 78%, whereas today the average is 0.05%.
claims.hypothesis: Response falls with a channel's age for all messages together, on top of the wear-out of any one idea. Falsified if the decline vanishes once each idea's own repetition is accounted for.
claims.rival: Average click rate by date, with repeated word sequences as the idea-level control. Neurons matter only for telling a repeated idea from repeated words.
claims.data: Upworthy Research Archive (dated randomised headline tests, 2013 to 2015, as in ME-24); Reddit resubmissions (ME-25). The 78% figure comes from a blog and needs a primary source.

claims.claim: Advertising spend stays near 1% of GDP whatever the channel, which the essay reads as a fixed human tolerance for advertising.
claims.quote: advertising has consistently hovered around 1% of GDP, implying a natural limit to our tolerance of ads, regardless of the channel
claims.hypothesis: The ratio of advertising spend to GDP shows no trend across the radio, television and internet eras and returns to about 1% after shocks.
claims.rival: No text method is needed: a published spend series answers it. The essay's own source is headed "Adspend busts out of the GDP corset", so the claim may already be false.
claims.data: National advertising spend and GDP by year and medium, from trade bodies and national accounts.

claims.claim: A meme's growth is set by its viral coefficient: the share of hosts who pass it on, times how many people each tells, times the share of those who take it up. Above 1 it grows exponentially.
claims.quote: This is a function of participation rate (how many hosts share), branching factor (how many they share it to) and infection rate
claims.hypothesis: A meme's viral coefficient measured in separate communities agrees across them more than different memes agree within one community, and content read before spread begins predicts it.
claims.rival: The first sharer's follower count and early share speed; hashtags; sentence embeddings; an LLM asked how shareable the post is. The coefficient itself comes from share counts, with no content method.
claims.data: Share cascades with timestamps and parent links from public research sets; the same meme cross-posted in several Reddit communities.

claims.claim: A share by one big account is not virality. Growth from a single broadcast dies quickly unless the people reached pass the meme on in turn.
claims.quote: it’ll die just as quickly if the audience doesn’t then start sharing with others
claims.hypothesis: At equal total reach, memes that spread through many person-to-person steps stay in circulation longer than memes whose reach came from one large broadcast.
claims.rival: None needed: the shape of the share tree and its timestamps answer it. Content methods enter only when asking which content produces long chains.
claims.data: Share trees with parent links and timestamps from public research sets of reposts.

claims.claim: After its peak a meme declines slowly as it is forgotten, and more slowly if it is memorable or its hosts wrote it down.
claims.quote: memes that are memorable, or get documented by their hosts, will survive longer
claims.hypothesis: Among memes matched on peak size and date, those given a durable written record (a reference entry, a book) keep a larger share of their peak ten years on.
claims.rival: Keyword and phrase counts over time (book and news word counts, search interest). No neurons needed unless the meme survives under new words.
claims.data: Phrase frequency series, with the date each meme first got a reference entry (Wikipedia, Know Your Meme). Reverse causation is the threat: memes that last get written down.

claims.claim: A declining meme recovers only when technology changes and it moves into a new medium, where it starts a new growth curve.
claims.quote: Only technological change can reverse the decline: mature memes jump to a new medium, riding a higher S-curve
claims.hypothesis: When a faded meme's share rebounds, the rebound is carried by works in a medium newer than the one it peaked in, more often than by works in the old medium.
claims.rival: Franchise names and keywords tracked across media; an LLM reading each synopsis. Words fail when the revived meme is renamed, which is where a unit that reads ideas could add something.
claims.data: Dated synopses across media: films, television, games, comics (Wikipedia, Wikidata). CJ-25's film series supplies the fades; the other media must be added.

claims.claim: People and firms copy and fight those already close to them and ignore those who are very different (Girard's mimetic rivalry).
claims.quote: We compete with those that are uncomfortably similar to us, and ignore those that are too different to worry about.
claims.hypothesis: The chance that one party copies or attacks another rises as the earlier distance between their content falls. Documented rivalries cluster among nearest neighbours, beyond what a shared industry or genre explains.
claims.rival: Word overlap between firms' product descriptions; industry codes; sentence embeddings. Words probably suffice, since rivals describe the same products.
claims.data: Firms' yearly self-descriptions with documented feature copying or lawsuits; franchises and authors with documented feuds, as in RX-S3.

claims.claim: Copying the majority feeds on itself: the common choice is stocked and seen more, so variety shrinks. The essay's case is car colour; its sources say the same of popular media.
claims.quote: This feedback loop means you’re less likely to see colorful cars on the road
claims.hypothesis: The spread of meme-unit profiles among each year's most popular works has narrowed over the decades, and the commonest variants gain share faster than random copying predicts.
claims.rival: The share of sequels and franchise entries among top films, which is the published evidence; word and embedding spread among the same works. Units must show more than a sequel count does.
claims.data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus plots with box office (5,665 per FI-28); PO-23's random-copying test for the second part.

claims.claim: A creator who wins an audience by being different then stops taking risks, because there is now something to lose, and drifts into the mainstream.
claims.quote: Fame brings fortune, so now you have something to lose. The safest move is to stop taking risks.
claims.hypothesis: Within one creator's career, each new work's distance from the mainstream of its year, and from the creator's own earlier work, falls after their audience jumps in size.
claims.rival: Novelty scored from words, embeddings or genre tags; an LLM asked how conventional each work is.
claims.data: Directors' films with box office (CMU corpus, Wikidata); authors or musicians with sales ranks. Compare with matched careers that had no breakout.

claims.claim: Going against the consensus usually fails, but the few who are different and right win big; following the consensus pays small and steady.
claims.quote: Most contrarians are wrong: the consensus view formed because it worked for most people in most situations.
claims.hypothesis: Works far from the mainstream of their year have lower median success than typical works but a higher chance of reaching the top 1%. Falsified if distance lowers both.
claims.rival: Novelty scored from genre tags, words or embeddings. CJ-21 and RX-23 test the average effect of novelty; this claim is about the spread of outcomes.
claims.data: Films with box office and budget (CMU corpus, Wikidata); papers with citation counts (OpenAlex).

claims.claim: Memes beget memes: each advance makes the next come sooner, so the rate of new ideas keeps rising. The essay repeats Kurzweil's figures of 5 times and 1,000 times faster.
claims.quote: Every advancement builds on those that came before, and gets us to where we’re going even faster.
claims.hypothesis: The number of first-appearing meme units, and of first-time pairings of units, per work rises decade on decade. Falsified if novelty per work is flat or falling.
claims.rival: New words and new word pairs per work; new pairings of patent classes. Any unit can test this. Some published measures on papers and patents are said to show the opposite (from memory; check).
claims.data: CJ-26's century of film plots (CMU corpus); patents and papers by year as other domains.

claims.claim: Cheap media connect everyone into one global pool of memes, where memes once passed mainly inside a tribe, religion or language.
claims.quote: Billions are lifted out of absolute poverty, and connected into the global meme pool.
claims.hypothesis: The share of variation in meme-unit frequencies that lies between national film industries (the Fst statistic) falls decade by decade. Falsified if it is flat.
claims.rival: The same statistic on word frequencies; counts of documented cross-border remakes.
claims.data: CMU film plots with country and year. PO-S4 compares industries by remake flow; this adds a trend over time.

claims.claim: Ideas reach the general public through early adopters, who mix both with innovators and with everyone else. Many later adopters trace back to them.
claims.quote: Bridging that gap are early adopters, who co-mingle with innovators, and spread infectious new ideas to the general population.
claims.hypothesis: Among carriers of an idea, the first sixth to adopt account for more of later adopters' exposure links than their number predicts, and they connect groups that are otherwise separate.
claims.rival: Keyword first-use dates on the same citation or follower graph. Neurons matter only if early carriers used different words from later ones.
claims.data: Papers with reference lists (OpenAlex, as in CE-25 and RX-26). A unit's first appearance per author gives the order of adoption.

claims.claim: Most ideas stall between early adopters and the early majority (the "chasm"); those that cross grow very fast. The essay credits the term to Christensen, though its source list cites the book Crossing the Chasm.
claims.quote: The difficult part of this journey is the leap from early adopters to the early majority.
claims.hypothesis: Final reach has two humps: memes either stop below about one sixth of their possible audience or go on to a majority, with few ending in between. Random copying predicts no gap.
claims.rival: Adoption curves from keywords, hashtags or genre tags. Any unit can test this.
claims.data: Unit frequency series by genre from FI-24 and PO-23 (CMU film plots); hashtag adoption series as a second domain.

claims.claim: Once the hype fades, what remains is decided by usefulness: useful ideas are remembered and recorded, and harmful or useless ones are actively forgotten.
claims.quote: Eventually the ‘hype cycle’ dies down, usefulness is all that’s left.
claims.hypothesis: A meme's rated practical usefulness predicts the share of its peak that it keeps five years later, and does not predict how high the peak was.
claims.rival: An LLM or human raters scoring usefulness from a short description; keyword counts for the frequency series. No neurons needed.
claims.data: Search and news frequency series for named methods, tools, challenges and fads, with usefulness rated blind to the outcome.

claims.claim: A dominant idea is not beaten by a better version of itself. It is displaced by something from a different category that makes the old category irrelevant.
claims.quote: new entrants almost never ‘beat’ incumbents in their own category: they make the category itself irrelevant
claims.hypothesis: When a dominant meme-unit profile loses share, the profiles that gain are further from it than its earlier, failed challengers were. Falsified if close variants take the share.
claims.rival: Genre or product-category tags; word and embedding distance. No neurons needed.
claims.data: Film genres over 80 years (CMU corpus); product categories with dated market shares.

claims.claim: Stories that evoke fear, anger, disgust or sadness are the most likely to be shared.
claims.quote: A study by Jonah Berger of New York Times headlines show these emotions are most likely to be shared and go viral.
claims.hypothesis: Within a randomised headline test, the version with more fear, anger, disgust or sadness wins more clicks. Test each emotion alone: the cited paper is usually read as finding that sadness lowers sharing (from memory; check).
claims.rival: Emotion word lists and a ready-made emotion classifier; an LLM rating each headline. These are cheap and already used on such data, so units must beat them on held-out tests.
claims.data: Upworthy Research Archive: 32,487 randomised headline tests (as in ME-24 and EN-25).

claims.claim: Headlines have grown more fearful and angry since 2000, and the essay says the cause is competition squeezing profit: institutions under pressure pander to base emotions.
claims.quote: as institutions get more desperate, they kowtow to the more base wants and desires of their audience
claims.hypothesis: Across outlets, the rise in negative-emotion content is larger where revenue or circulation fell more, and it begins after the fall, not before it.
claims.rival: The emotion labels from the study the essay cites, which came from a Transformer classifier; emotion word lists. No neurons needed.
claims.data: Dated headlines by outlet from 2000, joined to each outlet's circulation or revenue by year.

claims.claim: Much coverage is "filler" that adds nothing new, published because outlets must publish while waiting for an event. It can be told apart from real information.
claims.quote: If you can differentiate filler content from real information, you can get the timing right
claims.hypothesis: The share of an article's meme units that are new to its running story separates hand-labelled filler from news, and filler share peaks in the hours before scheduled events.
claims.rival: New words and new named entities against earlier coverage; embedding distance to earlier articles; an LLM asked what is new. Units must beat these when old content is merely reworded.
claims.data: Timestamped articles on running stories with scheduled events (election nights, finals), plus a hand-labelled sample of filler and news. US-25's drift measure is the nearest design.

claims.claim: Whoever first names a trend, or is its first credible source, is cited as the source by everyone who covers it afterwards.
claims.quote: coin a new term for an interesting trend, it’ll earn you references as the source or expert on the topic
claims.hypothesis: Among papers carrying an idea, later papers cite the one that coined its name more than earlier papers that carried the same idea unnamed, after allowing for venue and author fame.
claims.rival: Keyword first-use finds the coiner. Finding earlier carriers with no name needs a reader of ideas: sentence embeddings, or an LLM judging whether two abstracts state the same idea.
claims.data: Abstracts with reference lists and citation counts (OpenAlex, as in RX-25), plus a list of coined terms with first-use dates.

claims.claim: The same idea fails when it arrives too early and succeeds later. Timing, not content, separates the two (Pets.com in 1998, Chewy later).
claims.quote: Being early is the same as being wrong
claims.hypothesis: Among works carrying a set of meme units that later became common, the earliest carriers did worse against same-year peers than carriers at the middle of adoption.
claims.rival: First use of the idea's keywords or tags. Words miss early carriers that lacked the later name, so embeddings and an LLM judging "same idea?" are the rivals to beat.
claims.data: Films with box office (CMU corpus, as in FI-24); start-up descriptions with outcomes as a second domain.

claims.claim: Memes differ in infectiousness, retention and tendency to mutate. Highly infectious memes that give no real-world advantage burn out fast (the ice bucket challenge).
claims.quote: Some memes, like the ‘ice bucket challenge’, are highly infectious but burn out quickly, as they confer no real world advantage.
claims.hypothesis: Across memes matched on peak size, the faster the rise to the peak, the shorter the time to fall back to half of it.
claims.rival: Hashtag, phrase and search-interest counts. No neurons needed. A study of first names is said to show this pattern already (from memory; check).
claims.data: MemeTracker phrase clusters (as in ME-23); search-interest series for named memes; unit series from PO-23's film plots.

claims.claim: After a technology shift, whoever dominated the old way loses most and outsiders adapt fastest. Large bureaucracies enforce today's memes and miss the next ones.
claims.quote: Often its’ the most dominant species in the previous ecological niche that suffers the most in the transition to a new one
claims.hypothesis: After a dated change of medium, creators or firms whose output was most typical of the old medium take longer to carry the new medium's meme units, and lose more share, than peripheral ones.
claims.rival: Word and embedding distance to the old-medium average; firm size or earlier market share alone, with no text at all.
claims.data: Careers across a dated shift, such as silent to sound film or print to web publishing. Typicality is scored before the shift and adoption lag after it.

claims.claim: Change is speeding up, so no single meme lasts a career any more: the useful life of a meme keeps getting shorter.
claims.quote: you can no longer rely on finding one meme and milking that for the rest of your career
claims.hypothesis: The time a meme unit spends above half its peak share has shortened decade by decade. The neuron question is whether ideas turn over faster, or only the words for them.
claims.rival: The same lifetime measured on words, phrases and hashtags, where shortening is said to be reported already (from memory; check). Units add something only if their trend differs from the words'.
claims.data: Dated film plots (CMU corpus, PO-23); news headlines by year; book word counts for the word baseline.

claims.claim: When an idea goes mainstream it can come to stand for the opposite of what its creator meant. The essay's case: Fight Club, written as a warning, quoted with approval by the men it warned about.
claims.quote: Eventually new ideas go mainstream, and in some cases come to represent the opposite of what their creators intended.
claims.hypothesis: For widely quoted lines, the stance of the surrounding text moves away from that of the original passage as the quote spreads, and moves further the further it travels from its first audience.
claims.rival: Word overlap cannot see this, because the quoted words do not change. The rivals are a stance classifier and an LLM reading the surrounding passage.
claims.data: Famous quotes with their source passages, and dated public posts that quote them (Reddit archives; MemeTracker phrase contexts).

claims.claim: Attention is limited, so every new idea competes with all the others for it, and only the most useful, novel and interesting survive.
claims.quote: brain space is limited, and there's constant competition for our attention
claims.hypothesis: Content predicts which memes survive beyond a simulation where all memes are identical and only attention is limited. A large new meme also shortens the lives of others present at the time.
claims.rival: The content-free limited-attention model in the paper the essay cites; hashtag counts.
claims.data: ME-S3 already sets a content-free limited-attention simulation as its null; the displacement test would need dated social posts.

claims.claim: Frauds copy the outward signs of success (dress, polish, famous backers) without the activity behind them, and this mismatch is visible in advance.
claims.quote: Whenever someone is copying the ‘memes’ they associate with success, without carrying out the activites that actually lead to success, that’s a red flag.
claims.hypothesis: Before exposure, the public writing of firms later charged with fraud carries more success-stereotype memes, and fewer operational-detail memes, than matched firms never charged.
claims.rival: An LLM asked to rate 'image versus substance'; word lists of buzzwords and numbers.
claims.data: SEC enforcement releases to label firms; their earlier annual-report letters, press releases and archived websites; matched firms by sector and year.

claims.claim: Sayings spread by losing the clause that qualifies them ('great minds think alike' without its second line).
claims.quote: memes mutate over time, dropping parts that don’t benefit its survival, and picking up new components
claims.hypothesis: In clusters of copied quotations, variants that drop a qualifying clause gain share over the full form, more than length alone predicts.
claims.rival: Character length and word counts. Neurons are not needed to see truncation; only to say whether the dropped clause changed the meaning.
claims.data: MemeTracker quote clusters; Google Books n-grams for proverbs with and without their second line.

claims.claim: A variant whose meaning reverses the original can out-spread the original, so meaning in use drifts away from the author's.
claims.quote: If the opposite meaning is more likely to spread than the original, then it will
claims.hypothesis: Among copied quote variants, some meaning-changing variants reach more copies than the faithful form, and later uses take a stance opposite to the source passage.
claims.rival: An LLM judging whether two variants mean the same; sentence-embedding distance.
claims.data: MemeTracker quote variants; source passages for well-known misquotations.

claims.claim: The more a group's required belief departs from everyday reality, the more it binds members: costly beliefs signal and raise devotion.
claims.quote: the costlier the belief you hold on behalf of the group, the greater your devotion to the group

essays.name: The social benefits of bad beliefs

claims.hypothesis: Communities whose shared texts carry more reality-distant or costly belief content lose members more slowly than matched communities with cheaper beliefs.
claims.rival: An LLM rating how costly or implausible each community's stated beliefs are; human ratings.
claims.data: Member churn in online communities with post histories; published records of how long historical communes lasted and what they demanded.

claims.claim: Fringe beliefs persist because they act as a warning signal (aposematism: bright colours on poisonous animals) that deters recruitment and social demands.
claims.quote: Holding fringe beliefs makes it clear you’re not willing to be recruited for the cause

essays.name: The social benefits of bad beliefs

claims.hypothesis: After a user first posts fringe-belief content, approaches from mainstream groups (replies, invitations, mentions) fall compared with matched users who did not.
claims.rival: Keyword or community-membership flags for fringe content; any unit can supply the trigger.
claims.data: Public forum histories with reply graphs, before and after a user's first fringe post.

claims.claim: A group's memes are adopted as a package, not one at a time.
claims.quote: You can’t pick and choose the memes of the group, you must choose them all.
claims.hypothesis: Across people, the number of a group's signature memes a person carries is two-peaked (nearly all or nearly none), beyond what the memes' logical links predict.
claims.rival: Hashtag and keyword co-occurrence; topic models; survey answers.
claims.data: User post histories in political and fan communities; opinion surveys with many items.

claims.claim: Corrections to practical beliefs are welcomed; corrections to 'crony' beliefs (held to impress a group) are treated as attacks.
claims.quote: You aren’t upset they corrected you. The opposite is true for ‘crony’ beliefs
claims.hypothesis: Replies to a correction are more hostile when the corrected claim marks group identity than when it is a practical fact, at equal correction wording.
claims.rival: An LLM sorting claims into identity-marking or practical and scoring reply hostility; toxicity word lists.
claims.data: Fact-check notes and their replies on social platforms; debate forums with marked changes of view.

claims.claim: Being labelled a member of a group pushes a person toward that group's stereotype (Hacking's looping effect).
claims.quote: The more outsiders identify you as part of a group, the higher the pressure to conform to the stereotypes of that group.
claims.hypothesis: After others publicly label a user as belonging to a group, the user's own writing moves toward that group's typical meme profile, compared with matched unlabelled users.
claims.rival: Word-frequency distance or embedding distance to the group's average text.
claims.data: Forum histories with user flairs or labels applied by others, before and after the label.

claims.claim: After one post goes viral, a creator posts more and makes later posts resemble the viral one.
claims.quote: they start to post more, and make their future posts more like the post that went viral
claims.hypothesis: After a popularity shock, a creator's later posts move closer to the viral post than their earlier posts were, more than matched creators with no shock.
claims.rival: Word overlap and sentence-embedding distance to the viral post.
claims.data: Public post histories around a viral post; the essay's cited study reports half of shocks fade within 5 days.

claims.claim: Wide appeal and strong reaction trade off: the larger the audience, the blander the content has to be.
claims.quote: The only way to appeal to everybody, is to inspire passion from nobody
claims.hypothesis: As a creator's audience grows, their content moves toward the platform average and the spread of reactions to it (loved and hated) narrows.
claims.rival: Embedding distance to the platform centroid; word-rarity scores; rating variance needs no content unit.
claims.data: Creator histories with follower counts and reaction data; book or film ratings with full rating distributions.

claims.claim: A small group that refuses anything non-compliant sets the default for an indifferent majority when complying is cheap.
claims.quote: Only 2% of the U.S. population is Jewish, yet 41% of packaged food in the U.S. is certified kosher.
claims.hypothesis: A wording or content convention demanded by a small committed group becomes the majority form in mainstream outlets far beyond that group's population share, once compliance cost is low.
claims.rival: Keyword counts for the convention; no neurons needed when the convention has a fixed wording.
claims.data: Dated news archives and style guides for conventions with a known advocate group; product-label databases.

claims.claim: People assign labels by how well someone matches a category's memes, ignoring how common the category is (base-rate neglect).
claims.quote: In choosing the label of Librarian, based on the ‘memes’ of that profession, we’re committing what behavioral economist Daniel Kahneman calls ‘base rate neglect’.
claims.hypothesis: Human guesses of a described person's category follow the similarity between the description's meme profile and the category stereotype, with almost no weight on real base rates.
claims.rival: Sentence-embedding similarity to a stereotype description; an LLM asked the same question.
claims.data: Published base-rate-neglect vignettes with human answers; occupation counts from labour statistics.

claims.claim: Imitators copy what is visible without the mechanism, so they match the first version and then fall behind.
claims.quote: copycat companies almost never beat the original
claims.hypothesis: Copycat products match the original's meme profile at launch, then fail to track its later changes, and survive at lower rates than the originals.
claims.rival: Word overlap between product descriptions over time; survival needs no content unit.
claims.data: Documented clone products and their originals; archived product pages; company survival records.

claims.claim: Creators start by copying and diverge from their models as they gain skill.
claims.quote: Your route might be adjacent to others at first, but eventually your path will diverge as you find yourself.
claims.hypothesis: Within a career, the distance between a creator's work and its nearest earlier works by others rises from early to late works.
claims.rival: Sentence-embedding or word-overlap distance to nearest predecessors.
claims.data: Film plot summaries by director with release dates; song lyrics or novels by author career stage.

claims.claim: Seven subversion tactics listed by a Soviet defector, such as stoking division over trivial issues, are still in use.
claims.quote: Divide the people into hostile groups by constantly harping on controversial issues of no importance.
claims.hypothesis: Posts from documented state-run influence accounts carry these tactic themes, on both sides of a dispute, at higher rates than matched ordinary accounts.
claims.rival: An LLM given the list of seven tactics and asked to tag each post; topic keywords.
claims.data: Platform-released archives of state-linked accounts; matched samples of ordinary accounts from the same period.

claims.claim: Much propaganda is dull or absurd on purpose: making people repeat it shows the regime's power, so persuasion is not its aim.
claims.quote: The greater the absurdity of the required performance, the more clearly it demonstrates that the regime can make most people obey
claims.hypothesis: Official messaging from more coercive regimes is rated less persuasive and more implausible than messaging from less coercive ones on the same subject.
claims.rival: Human or LLM ratings of plausibility and persuasiveness; neurons add nothing obvious.
claims.data: Translated state-media corpora; published indices of state repression by country and year.

claims.claim: Media coverage of a crime raises the chance of copies (a 'memetic crime loop'); showing that something is possible invites replication.
claims.quote: once it’s out there in the media, the information causes more damage to be done
claims.hypothesis: Incidents of a crime type cluster after heavy coverage of one, and later cases repeat incidental details of the covered case more than of uncovered cases.
claims.rival: Incident counts against coverage volume need no content unit; keyword match on method details.
claims.data: Dated incident databases; news archive volume per incident; published statements by perpetrators.

claims.claim: Violence follows an exchange of words, and which words are used changes the odds of escalation.
claims.quote: The words you choose to use in this exchange can radically alter your chances of getting punched.
claims.hypothesis: Early turns of a conversation contain content that forecasts whether it later turns into personal attack, beyond politeness markers.
claims.rival: Politeness and insult word lists; an LLM reading the opening turns; sentence embeddings.
claims.data: Public datasets of online conversations labelled for later derailment into personal attacks.

claims.claim: A stock that becomes a meme is priced by the cause it stands for, not by the business.
claims.quote: The stock no longer represented the underlying value of a video game retailer, it represented a way to “stick it to the man”.
claims.hypothesis: For meme stocks, growth in posts framing the stock as a cause predicts retail buying and price better than growth in posts arguing valuation.
claims.rival: Ticker mention counts; sentiment word lists; an LLM sorting posts into cause or valuation.
claims.data: Archived trading-forum posts from 2019 to 2021; daily price and retail volume series.

claims.claim: Conspicuously good people are attacked, and on dimensions unrelated to their good act, most of all by status rivals.
claims.quote: When someone is unimpeachable along one dimension, they’re attacked along unrelated dimensions
claims.hypothesis: Replies to public announcements of generosity contain more criticism on unrelated topics than replies to matched neutral announcements, and more still from the announcer's peers.
claims.rival: An LLM tagging each reply as on-topic or off-topic criticism; toxicity scores.
claims.data: Public donation or good-deed announcements with reply threads; the essay cites lab studies putting such punishment near 20%.

claims.claim: Virtue that costs status at the time is an honest signal; virtue that pays off at once is not.
claims.quote: look for those who are willing to be pariahs in the short term to achieve long term goals
claims.hypothesis: Value statements that differ from what peers were saying at the time predict later conduct better than statements matching the fashionable consensus.
claims.rival: Sentence-embedding distance from the peer-group average statement in the same year.
claims.data: Dated corporate value and mission statements; later violation or fraud records for the same firms.

claims.claim: At equal rank, someone who fits the stereotype of their profession is likely to be worse at it than someone who does not.
claims.quote: If someone looks like a stereotype for their profession, that’s a sign they may not very good at it.
claims.hypothesis: Among professionals of equal rank, the more stereotype-typical the self-presentation text, the lower the objective performance.
claims.rival: Embedding distance to the profession's average bio; an LLM rating typicality.
claims.data: Professional bios or pitch texts paired with outcome records, within one rank or funding stage.

claims.claim: Once a marker of talent is widely known, imitators adopt it and it stops predicting talent.
claims.quote: any sufficiently popular trope can and will be used against us
claims.hypothesis: The link between a marker meme and success weakens as the marker's share of all texts rises.
claims.rival: Keyword frequency of the marker against outcome, by year.
claims.data: Dated startup pitches or job profiles with outcomes; headline tests for the click version.

claims.claim: Status beliefs start among the rich, spread downward, and are dropped by the rich once the wider public adopts them.
claims.quote: When these ‘mind viruses’ get copied by the lower classes, because they have become aspirational, they’re summarily abandoned
claims.hypothesis: A meme's frequency in elite outlets falls after its frequency in mass outlets rises, more often than the reverse order.
claims.rival: Keyword time series for named beliefs; neurons only matter where the belief is reworded.
claims.data: Dated archives of elite and mass-market publications; baby-name records by parental income as a non-text check.

claims.claim: Because well-connected people are over-represented among anyone's contacts (the friendship paradox), what they display looks more common than it is.
claims.quote: your friends are likely to be on average richer than you are, and that skews your estimations
claims.hypothesis: A meme's prevalence as seen in users' feeds exceeds its true prevalence in proportion to how well connected its carriers are.
claims.rival: Hashtag or keyword counts on a follower graph; no content unit beyond that is required.
claims.data: Follower graphs with post content; surveys of perceived against actual prevalence.

claims.claim: In young markets a brand's own messages are scattered; in mature markets they are consistent.
claims.quote: If you ask employees why customers buy, they all give different reasons.
claims.hypothesis: The spread of meme profiles across one firm's pages and over successive versions of its homepage falls as the firm's product category ages.
claims.rival: TF-IDF or embedding variance across the same pages.
claims.data: Archived company websites by year; category founding dates from company databases.

claims.claim: Using the same message on every channel ('memetic alignment') raises purchases and referrals.
claims.quote: you use all the same words in your sales calls, emails, blogs and social posts, you’ll have memetic alignment
claims.hypothesis: Campaigns whose advert and landing page share more memes convert better than campaigns with the same advert and a less matching page.
claims.rival: Plain word overlap between advert and page, which is what the essay literally recommends.
claims.data: Crowdfunding pages (title, blurb, body) with funding outcomes; private advert and landing-page pairs with conversion rates.

claims.claim: Attention is so limited that a message carrying one idea beats a message carrying several.
claims.quote: you will be very lucky to get more than one idea through
claims.hypothesis: Within a randomised headline test, the arm with fewer distinct memes wins more clicks, with length held fixed.
claims.rival: Word count; an LLM counting the ideas in each headline.
claims.data: Archived randomised headline tests with click counts.

claims.claim: A counter-meme (Godwin's law) made Nazi comparisons backfire on whoever uses them.
claims.quote: making Nazi comparisons now acts more to weaken your own position, than that of your intended target
claims.hypothesis: In forum threads, replies making a Nazi or Hitler comparison score lower than matched replies in the same thread, and the comparison's rate per reply fell in communities after Godwin's law became widely quoted there.
claims.rival: A plain word search for 'Nazi' and 'Hitler' finds the literal cases. A neuron reader only earns a place on indirect comparisons with neither word, and must beat an LLM reading the reply.
claims.data: Usenet and Reddit archives with reply scores and dates; first mentions of 'Godwin' per community as the exposure date. Availability to be checked.

claims.claim: Warning people before they meet a false claim works; correcting them afterwards barely does.
claims.quote: once someone is exposed, debunking has little effect
claims.hypothesis: Accounts that saw a warning or refutation before first meeting a false claim repeat it later, in any wording, less often than matched accounts that saw the same refutation only after exposure.
claims.rival: No neurons needed for the main test. Matching reworded repeats of a claim needs a reader; sentence embeddings or an LLM matcher are the cheap candidates.
claims.data: A randomised prebunking experiment, or public Community Notes data using the timing of a note relative to each account's first exposure. Observational timing is confounded; say so.

claims.claim: Each extra message in an advert dilutes the others; more than three claims breeds doubt.
claims.quote: the more messages you try and communicate in your advertising, the less likelihood there is of any single message being communicated
claims.hypothesis: Within one randomised headline test, the version carrying fewer distinct ideas wins more clicks, with length held fixed, and the penalty steepens past three ideas.
claims.rival: An LLM asked to count the separate claims in each headline, plus word count and clause count. Counting active neuron units is only one more way to count.
claims.data: The archived Upworthy randomised headline tests already used by the fitness designs.

claims.claim: People improve things by adding, and rarely by taking away, even when taking away works as well.
claims.quote: we overlook opportunities to subtract to solve a problem, even when advantageous
claims.hypothesis: Along documented revision or adaptation links, the later version gains more ideas than it drops. Retelling from memory should show the reverse (loss), so the two processes are separable.
claims.rival: Word count and length change between versions. Units matter only if idea count and word count disagree.
claims.data: Wikipedia article revision histories; film remakes and sequels paired with their originals; the study's source-to-adaptation pairs.

claims.claim: Beliefs and institutions change mainly in crises; in stable times people keep following existing trails.
claims.quote: The only time things really change is under conditions of uncertainty.
claims.hypothesis: The yearly rate at which new ideas enter a body of text and old ones leave is higher in dated crisis years (war, recession, pandemic) than in neighbouring stable years.
claims.rival: Turnover of vocabulary or topic-model topics per year. Any unit can test this; neurons must show a pattern that word turnover misses.
claims.data: Film plots by release year; news headlines by date; founding dates of organisations in Wikidata against war and recession years.

claims.claim: True corrections travel more slowly on social media than the false claims they correct.
claims.quote: Facts spread slower than misinformation on social media, and people often believe even after debunking.
claims.hypothesis: For claims paired with their fact-checks, the fact-check reaches fewer accounts and takes longer to reach a fixed audience than the claim, after controlling for the poster's follower count.
claims.rival: Share counts need no neurons. Pairing a reworded claim with its fact-check does need a reader: sentence embeddings or an LLM matcher are the bar.
claims.data: Public fact-check collections linked to posts; Community Notes data. The pairing step could reuse seed US-S3.

claims.claim: It is easier to start believing a claim once doubted than to stop believing one once accepted.
claims.quote: are better able to believe in a claim once thought to be false, as opposed to unbelieving something once believed to be true
claims.hypothesis: After a paper is retracted, later papers keep carrying its ideas at close to the earlier rate, while after a doubted result is confirmed its ideas are taken up quickly.
claims.rival: Citation counts before and after retraction. A content reader is needed only to see the idea carried without a citation; embeddings or an LLM reader are the rivals.
claims.data: A public retraction database joined to citing papers' abstracts. Availability and coverage to be checked.

claims.claim: Types of crime spread by imitation among susceptible people, rise as waves, then burn out.
claims.quote: crime exists as memetic loops that propagate throughout the most susceptible members of the population
claims.hypothesis: After a heavily reported act of one type, acts of the same type rise above baseline for a limited period, and the rise scales with the amount of coverage, not with the act's severity.
claims.rival: Event counts and coverage counts need no neurons at all. This is a contagion test on dated incidents.
claims.data: Dated incident databases for one crime type plus news coverage volume. Sensitive material; use counts only.

claims.claim: A little friction stops a harmful act without people switching to a substitute.
claims.quote: That catastrophic acts can be prevented with small amounts of friction is a clue to their nature as a temporary mind virus
claims.hypothesis: After a platform bans a term or community, the idea itself (in any wording) falls nearly as much as the banned words do, in the same accounts. Displacement into new wording would falsify it.
claims.rival: Keyword counts cannot see reworded substitutes, so they cannot test displacement. The bar is sentence embeddings or an LLM reading posts for the idea.
claims.data: Public Reddit archives around documented community bans; the same accounts before and after.

claims.claim: A moderate penalty selects for forms that slip under it; only a ruinous penalty ends the behaviour.
claims.quote: When we set a penalty for corruption, we’ve unknowingly added selection pressure to the system.
claims.hypothesis: In a loop that breeds text to carry an idea past a detector, a weak penalty yields variants that keep the idea and evade the detector; a harsh penalty makes the idea disappear from the population.
claims.rival: Run the same loop against a keyword filter, an embedding classifier and an LLM reader as the detector. A neuron detector must be evaded less often at equal cost.
claims.data: Generated text populations; related designs US-21 and seed US-S9 already test gaming of a score.

claims.claim: A funny correction stops people passing the rumour on. The essay quotes a minister's assertion; no data is given.
claims.quote: everybody who have seen this clarification through the community will never share the original disinformation again
claims.hypothesis: Among corrections of the same false claim, those rated funnier are shared more widely and are followed by a larger drop in repeats of the claim.
claims.rival: An LLM or human rating of how funny each correction is. No neurons required.
claims.data: Fact-check posts and replies to one claim with share counts; funniness rated blind. A suitable public set is still to be found.

claims.claim: Jokes are funniest when they join concepts that are far apart, because that breaks expectation.
claims.quote: words or concepts that are linguistically far apart, are the funniest, as they violate expectations
claims.hypothesis: Within one cartoon, captions whose active units rarely occur together in ordinary text are rated funnier. This runs against H32, which says clashing memes repel.
claims.rival: Distance between the caption's words in a word-embedding model, which is how the cited kind of study measures it, plus an LLM judge.
claims.data: Crowd-rated cartoon caption contests, as in seed FI-S3.

claims.claim: We copy people who are like us but one step ahead, not anyone with status.
claims.quote: They must be similar enough to us for their desires to be relevant, but they must possess some quality or status that we do not.
claims.hypothesis: Uptake of a new idea is highest from sources in the adopter's own field with moderately higher standing, and lower from both peers of equal standing and distant stars.
claims.rival: Citation or follower counts alone as the status measure, and shared words as the uptake measure.
claims.data: The exposure and adoption records planned for RX-26, with a similarity and status gap added for each pair.

claims.claim: High-status people drop a fashion as it becomes common, and the abandonment cascades down.
claims.quote: Celebrities are incentivised to continually differentiate themselves, giving up on a fashion just as it becomes fashionable.
claims.hypothesis: A meme's use by high-status sources peaks and falls before its use by everyone else, and its overall decline is led by the top tier.
claims.rival: The same timing test on words, names or hashtags. Any unit can test it.
claims.data: Dated text with a status measure for each author: research papers by lab standing, or posts by follower tier. Baby names by parents' income are a non-text check.

claims.claim: People also define themselves against disliked others by doing the opposite.
claims.quote: we’ll often decide to take the opposite action of someone that we dislike
claims.hypothesis: When a disliked rival group starts using an idea, the home group's use of it falls relative to ideas the rival did not adopt. Girard's 'rivals become doubles' (seed RX-S3) predicts the opposite.
claims.rival: Counts of partisan phrases, which is how party language is already measured. Units help only when the same idea is worded differently by each side.
claims.data: Legislative speeches labelled by party and date; could share data with seed RX-S8.

claims.claim: Information wrapped in a story is far more likely to be remembered and passed on.
claims.quote: Adding narrative in this way makes information 6 to 7 times more likely to be retained
claims.hypothesis: In retelling chains, a set of facts survives more steps when embedded in a story than when given as a list of the same facts.
claims.rival: An LLM or human coder counting which facts appear in each retelling. No neurons required.
claims.data: Retelling chains (human or model) seeded with matched story and list versions; could be added to CE-21.

claims.claim: Memory is a quality filter: what you recall of a draft without looking is the good part.
claims.quote: throw away your first draft: trust your brain to remember the good parts
claims.hypothesis: The parts of a text that survive a rewrite from memory are the parts blind readers rated highest beforehand, more than chance and more than the parts a second writer keeps when editing with the text in view.
claims.rival: An LLM asked directly which passages are best; passage position and length.
claims.data: Short drafts rated passage by passage, then rewritten from memory by people or models.

claims.claim: People take on the ideas of those they spend most time with.
claims.quote: you’re the average of the five people you spend the most time with, and this can only be because you’re taking on their memes
claims.hypothesis: A person's later writing moves toward the idea profile of their most frequent contacts, more than toward matched people they did not interact with.
claims.rival: Shared vocabulary and sentence-embedding similarity between the person and their contacts.
claims.data: An email archive or follower graph with dated text, as in seed RX-S11.

claims.claim: Some harmful ideas weaken resistance and open the way to worse ones.
claims.quote: some bad memes open the door to worse ones
claims.hypothesis: Adopting idea A raises the chance of later adopting idea B more than adopting B raises the chance of A, and more than baseline, in the same accounts.
claims.rival: Order of joining communities or first use of keywords. Units matter only for ideas expressed without their usual words; embeddings are the bar there.
claims.data: Public long-run posting histories by account, with dated first appearances of each idea.

claims.claim: Anniversaries and rituals keep a meme alive by refreshing it on a schedule.
claims.quote: we have specific dates in the calendar to remember the Holocaust, World War II, or Independence Day, in part to keep refreshing healthy memes
claims.hypothesis: Events with a fixed commemoration date fade from public text more slowly over decades than events of similar initial coverage without one.
claims.rival: Keyword and page-view counts by year are enough. No neurons required.
claims.data: News archives or encyclopedia page views for matched historical events with and without an annual observance.

claims.claim: A rumour spreads only after losing detail (levelling), exaggerating what remains (sharpening) and bending toward the group's outlook (assimilation).
claims.quote: the initial story must be distorted in 3 directions to make a good rumour
claims.hypothesis: Along retelling chains the number of active units falls, the surviving units fire more strongly, and content shifts toward the retelling group's usual units. Versions showing all three are passed on most.
claims.rival: Word counts for levelling, and an LLM listing and grading each retelling's statements for sharpening and assimilation.
claims.data: The retelling chains planned in ME-22 and CE-22, with groups of retellers given different backgrounds.

claims.claim: A superstition survives only if obeying it is cheap compared with the threatened penalty.
claims.quote: Believing the rumour has to incur very little relative cost, compared to the purported benefits
claims.hypothesis: Across a catalogue of superstitions, those with a low cost of compliance relative to the stated penalty are more widespread and longer lived.
claims.rival: An LLM or human coder rating each superstition's cost and penalty. No neurons required.
claims.data: A folklore catalogue of superstitions with some measure of prevalence or age. Source still to be found.

claims.claim: Denying a rumour with evidence strengthens it; replacing it with a different story works. The first half (the 'backfire effect') is contested.
claims.quote: Instead you must give them a new story to believe
claims.hypothesis: Corrections that supply an alternative account are followed by a larger fall in repeats of the claim than bare denials, and bare denials are followed by no fall or a rise.
claims.rival: An LLM classifying each correction as denial or alternative story; keyword or link matching to count repeats.
claims.data: Fact-checks of one claim family with dated repeats of the claim before and after each.

claims.claim: Vague posts are read as profound when a high-status person writes them.
claims.quote: users defer to high status individuals who post ambiguously
claims.hypothesis: Vagueness raises engagement for high-status accounts and lowers it for low-status accounts: an interaction, not a main effect of either.
claims.rival: An LLM rating of how vague each post is, with follower count as status. No neurons required.
claims.data: Public posts with engagement and follower counts; a sharper version of seed CJ-S10.

claims.claim: Reading widely protects against false claims; a narrow, repeated diet makes people adopt them.
claims.quote: Consuming a wide variety of news sources can help give you a wider perspective with which to judge new information against
claims.hypothesis: Accounts that draw on more varied sources before a false claim appears are less likely to repeat it afterwards than accounts with a concentrated diet, at equal activity.
claims.rival: A count of distinct sources or communities per account. Matching repeats of the claim needs keywords or embeddings, not neurons.
claims.data: Public posting histories with links or community membership, and dated flagged claims.

claims.claim: Calm wording gets the other side to engage, so the message travels beyond its own camp.
claims.quote: Moderating your language makes the opposite side more likely to engage, increasing the reach outside your own echo chamber
claims.hypothesis: With topic and author held fixed, posts with less emotional wording draw a larger share of their engagement from the opposing camp.
claims.rival: Emotion word lists and an LLM rating of tone. No neurons required.
claims.data: Political posts where the leaning of each engaging account can be estimated.

claims.claim: There is a class of information ('antimemes') that people take in but will not pass on.
claims.quote: any piece of information which you wouldn't share with anybody, like passwords, taboos and dirty secrets
claims.hypothesis: Some content features predict a low ratio of shares to views: an item is read as much as others but shared far less. It mirrors seed ME-S6, which looks for a 'pass this on' unit.
claims.rival: An LLM rating how embarrassing or taboo an item is; topic tags.
claims.data: Any outlet that publishes both most-viewed and most-shared lists, or posts with view and share counts.

claims.claim: An idea can be killed by a bigger one that takes its attention.
claims.quote: ideas can be killed “with better ideas”
claims.hypothesis: A news story's coverage decays faster when a larger story breaks within a few days than it does for matched stories with no such competitor.
claims.rival: Counts of repeated phrases or keywords per day, the standard way news cycles are tracked. No neurons required.
claims.data: A dated archive of news quotes and phrases, such as the one behind ME-23.

claims.claim: Making something sound dull or ordinary stops people noticing and spreading it.
claims.quote: name committees something boring so that nobody will look too closely at it
claims.hypothesis: With content fixed, the least novel title for an item draws the least attention. This is the low-novelty arm of the inverted U that CJ-21 already tests.
claims.rival: An LLM rating of dullness and word-level surprise (how predictable the title is to a language model).
claims.data: Randomised headline tests, as in CJ-21.

claims.claim: A small change in wording can change an idea's spread a great deal. This contradicts H30, where small variants move results 1 to 2%.
claims.quote: even a slight change in narrative can make a huge difference in terms of an idea’s evolutionary fitness
claims.hypothesis: Among headline pairs that differ by a few words, the click gap is large when the edit changes which units fire and small when it does not.
claims.rival: Word edit distance and sentence-embedding distance between the two headlines.
claims.data: Randomised headline tests with near-identical arms, as in seed CJ-S5.

claims.claim: A phrase carries its meme only for readers who share the culture behind it; jargon compresses meaning for insiders and is noise to outsiders.

essays.name: The cure for the common meme

claims.hypothesis: The same phrase activates a meme's neurons only when the surrounding text sets up the shared culture, and not when it appears out of place.
claims.rival: Keyword counts cannot do this at all. The real rivals are a context-aware embedding of the phrase and an LLM reading the passage.

claims.claim: New technology carries over features of the old that it no longer needs (skeuomorphs): the floppy-disk save icon, the camera shutter click.
claims.hypothesis: Carried-over features act as markers of descent, showing which older technology a newer one came from.
claims.rival: A keyword list of the old technology's parts.

claims.claim: Businesses that care about small details also get the big things right, so an incidental cue such as napkin thickness predicts customer satisfaction.
claims.quote: you can reliably predict customer satisfaction with a restaurant by the thickness of the napkins
claims.hypothesis: In restaurant reviews, what reviewers say about incidental details (napkins, cutlery, floors) predicts the venue's overall rating and its official hygiene score, even with all comments about the food removed.
claims.rival: Counts of detail words, or an LLM asked to score each review's remarks on incidental details. Either should be enough; no look inside a model is needed.
claims.data: Public review text (for example the Yelp Open Dataset) joined to a city's published restaurant inspection scores. Availability and licence to confirm.

claims.claim: A longer description makes the same idea seem more creative.
claims.quote: Ideas presented with longer descriptions are perceived as more creative than shorter ones.
claims.hypothesis: When one idea is written up short and long, blind raters score the long version as more creative. Neuron units (neurons used as the measuring unit for an idea) are needed only to confirm both versions carry the same idea.
claims.rival: Word count alone. If length predicts creativity ratings as well as any content measure, the content measure adds nothing.
claims.data: New: about 100 ideas, each written at two lengths by an LLM and rated blind by a paid panel.

claims.claim: People judge a product by what surrounds it, so changing a cue around an unchanged product (price, brand, packaging, music) changes how good it seems.
claims.quote: our imputation of quality can be hacked. Small changes often cause big changes in behavior.
claims.hypothesis: The same passage is rated higher when presented with prestige cues (a known publisher, a high price) than with shabby ones, and the size of the shift is predictable from the cue.
claims.rival: An LLM asked to rate the passage under each presentation. If its ratings move as people's do, reading neurons adds nothing.
claims.data: New: identical passages shown under randomly assigned presentations to a paid panel. FI-25 and EN-S10 change the content; this changes only the wrapper.

claims.claim: A rebrand keeps its customers if the new name and mascot stay as close as possible in meaning to the old ones (Charmin's bear to Cushelle's koala, no sales lost) and loses them otherwise (Germany, sales down 21%).
claims.quote: finding a new set of ‘memes’ that were as close as possible to what consumers expected from Charmin
claims.hypothesis: Across documented rebrands, the distance between old and new brand assets (name, mascot, pack wording) predicts the fall in sales or search interest afterwards: the smaller the distance, the smaller the fall.
claims.rival: Human similarity ratings of old and new assets; sentence or image embeddings; spelling and sound distance between the two names.
claims.data: A list of documented rebrands with sales before and after. Sales are mostly private; Google Trends interest is public. The sample is likely to be a few dozen.

claims.claim: Brands in an embarrassing product category converge on the same reassuring symbols, children and animals, and this is specific to cultures where the topic is taboo.
claims.quote: near every UK toilet roll brand has a baby, toddler, or animal on the packaging
claims.hypothesis: Packs in categories that people rate as embarrassing carry child or animal imagery more often than packs in other categories, and more often in countries where the topic is rated more taboo.
claims.rival: Human tags of pack images, or labels from an off-the-shelf image-labelling model. Counting tags is all the test needs.
claims.data: Pack images from supermarket websites in several countries; embarrassment ratings from a short survey.

claims.claim: The sounds in a brand name carry associations of their own, so an invented name can inherit a predecessor's feel by sounding like it.
claims.quote: The soft “Ch” consonant cluster sounds French to British consumers, and therefore takes on an air of sophistication, femininity, and elegance.
claims.hypothesis: People's ratings of invented names (soft, feminine, French, sophisticated) are predictable from the name's sounds, and two names that sound alike get similar ratings.
claims.rival: A classifier on letter and sound sequences; an LLM asked to rate each name. A neuron reading of a made-up name would have to beat both.
claims.data: New: a few hundred invented names rated by a paid panel in two countries.

claims.claim: Memes about a film on social media decide its box office: affectionate memes lifted Minions: The Rise of Gru, mocking memes sank Morbius.
claims.quote: Today we see the popularity of the films themselves being dictated by the memes circulated on social media.
claims.hypothesis: Before release, the volume of memes about a film predicts opening box office beyond budget and franchise. With volume held fixed, a higher share of mocking memes predicts a lower take.
claims.rival: Hashtag and keyword counts for volume; an LLM reading each post for tone. Tone is a judgement an LLM reader already makes well.
claims.data: Pre-release social posts per film (archive access to confirm), with public box-office and budget figures.

claims.claim: Life imitates art: after a hit film about a profession, real members of that profession take up its dress, talk and attitudes, and recruitment rises (Wall Street, The Godfather, Top Gun).
claims.quote: it wasn’t common to dress or act like Gordon Gekko until after the film Wall St came out
claims.hypothesis: After a hit film about a profession, non-fiction about that profession (news, memoirs, trade press) carries more of the film's distinctive neuron units than before release, compared with control professions and matched flops.
claims.rival: Counts of the film's catchphrases and props; sentence-embedding similarity to the film's plot summary. Both catch quoted uptake; units must show uptake without the film's words.
claims.data: Dated news and book text around release years; recruitment figures as a behavioural check. FI-28 and PO-S5 ask a similar question inside films only.

claims.claim: Heavy advertising is a costly signal that only makers of good products can afford, like a peacock's tail.
claims.quote: companies can’t afford to spend a lot on advertising if their products aren’t good enough

essays.name: A weed with an advertising budget

claims.hypothesis: Within a product category, brands that spend more on advertising score higher on independent quality tests, and the link is stronger for expensive public media than for cheap targeted adverts.
claims.rival: No content measure is involved: advertising spend against independent test scores.
claims.data: Advertising-spend estimates (mostly commercial) and independent product-test ratings by category.

claims.claim: When every advertiser pays the same for the slot, the adverts that get shared and remembered are the most creative, funny and emotional ones.
claims.quote: Every advertiser pays the same for the Superbowl advertising slot, but it’s the most creative, funny, emotional adverts that get shared

essays.name: A weed with an advertising budget

claims.hypothesis: Among Super Bowl adverts of one year, humour and emotion read from the advert's script predict online shares and viewer-poll rank. The slot price is equal by design, so spend cannot explain the spread.
claims.rival: An LLM rating each script for funny, emotional and creative; human tags; sentence embeddings.
claims.data: Scripts or descriptions of Super Bowl adverts by year, with public viewer-poll rankings and online view counts. Sources to confirm.

claims.claim: A visual style signals quality only while it is costly to make. Once free stock photos, stock illustration or AI art make it cheap, leading firms move to a costlier style.
claims.quote: expect the vibe to shift again to something costlier

essays.name: A weed with an advertising budget

claims.hypothesis: After a style becomes cheap to produce, the fastest-growing firms stop using it sooner than other firms: its share falls among leaders while it rises overall.
claims.rival: Human style tags, or style labels from an off-the-shelf image-labelling model, on archived home pages. Vision-model neurons would have to beat those labels.
claims.data: Archived start-up home pages by year, with funding or growth data, and the launch dates of free stock-photo sites and AI image tools.

claims.claim: Quality is fractal: a small piece of a product shows the quality of the whole.
claims.quote: you can make a good judgement about an entire product by looking at a small piece of it

essays.name: A weed with an advertising budget

claims.hypothesis: A rating of a short random excerpt predicts the rating of the whole work almost as well as a second rating of the whole work does.
claims.rival: An LLM rating the excerpt; simple word statistics of the excerpt. Any reader can run this test.
claims.data: Full texts with public ratings, such as public-domain books or openly licensed fiction with reader scores. Source to confirm.

claims.claim: Few products spread unaided, because that needs a viral coefficient above 1: each user must recruit at least one more. Most need broadcast advertising.
claims.quote: a product has to be so memorable and shareable that it maintains a viral coefficient above 1
