essays.name: A weed with an advertising budget

claims.hypothesis: In sharing data, nearly all items have a reproduction number (new sharers per sharer) below 1, and most of an item's reach comes directly from broadcast sources, not from chains of person-to-person sharing.
claims.rival: No content measure is involved: count the shape of sharing chains.
claims.data: Public sharing-chain datasets with who-shared-from-whom links. Source to confirm.

claims.claim: Small incongruities each reduce trust a little, and past some number the customer switches to active suspicion.
claims.quote: Every small incongruity you find, chips away at your trust. If enough of them add up, you begin an active investigation.
claims.hypothesis: Trust ratings fall with each incongruous cue added to a description, gently at first and then sharply past a threshold number, not in a straight line.
claims.rival: A count of incongruities flagged by an LLM reader or by human tags.
claims.data: New: service descriptions with zero to six planted incongruities, rated for trust by a paid panel. H32 says clashing memes repel; this asks for the shape of the curve.

claims.claim: Surface cues pick out the very worst and the very best providers, but not the middle, where those rising and those declining look the same.
claims.quote: those on their way up, and on their way down, often exhibit the same behaviors
claims.hypothesis: Visible cues mentioned in reviews predict hidden quality (inspection results, later closure) well for the top and bottom fifths of venues and near chance for the middle three fifths.
claims.rival: Counts of cue words; cue tags from an LLM reader.
claims.data: The review and inspection data of the napkin test, with later closures added.

claims.claim: We attend only to what the brain did not already predict.
claims.quote: our senses only look for information when they notice something the brain didn’t already predict
claims.hypothesis: The parts of a story a language model predicts worst are the parts people recall and pass on. Surprise measured in neuron units predicts recall beyond surprise measured word by word.
claims.rival: Word-by-word surprisal: how unexpected each word is, read from the model's ordinary output with no look inside. Word rarity is a second cheap rival.
claims.data: Coded human recall of stories, such as the Berl et al. data listed under CE-21 (OSF 72v3f).

claims.claim: Minds are tuned to threats, because a false alarm costs minutes and a miss costs a life.
claims.quote: If I’m wrong about the tiger, I waste a few minutes running away.
claims.hypothesis: Statements about threats survive retelling more often than neutral statements of equal length, and neuron units for threat predict which statements survive.
claims.rival: A list of threat and negative words; threat tags from an LLM reader.
claims.data: Berl et al. coded recall, as in CE-21, which already tests survival and negative-content effects.

claims.claim: Memory for brands is tiny: two or three brands per category and one or two facts about each.
claims.quote: Customers rarely know more than 2-3 brands in any given category, don’t know more than 1-2 things about each brand
claims.hypothesis: In free recall the median person names three or fewer brands per category and two or fewer attributes per brand. In public text, one or two neuron units account for most of a brand's distinctive profile.
claims.rival: Survey counts; the words that most often sit beside the brand name; an LLM asked to list the brand's associations.
claims.data: A new free-recall survey on a paid panel; public text that mentions brands, such as product reviews.

claims.claim: A brand's share of Google searches among its competitors predicts 83% of its market share.
claims.quote: share of search – your brand’s Google search data relative to a basket of competitors – can reliably predict 83% of a brand’s market share
claims.hypothesis: A brand's share of category searches tracks its market share, and changes in search share come before changes in market share. Counting unnamed references to the brand as well adds nothing over counting its name.
claims.rival: Share of search is itself a keyword count, so it is the rival. Neurons could only add by catching mentions that omit the name.
claims.data: Google Trends series for brand names; published market shares by category and year.

claims.claim: A brand whose share of voice exceeds its share of market grows until the two are equal.
claims.quote: generating excess share of voice – your mind share if bigger than your market share – reliably drives growth, as the two eventually equalize
claims.hypothesis: A brand, or a story meme, whose share of mentions this period exceeds its share of adoption gains adoption share next period, and the gap closes over time.
claims.rival: Name counts for brands and keyword counts for memes. Any measure of presence can run the test.
claims.data: Brands: advertising share and market share (mostly commercial data). Memes: share of press mentions against share of new films carrying the meme.

claims.claim: Cultural codes, not the object, set perceived value: bargain shoes in a fake luxury shop were praised and sold for hundreds of dollars.
claims.quote: The right cultural codes can completely transform the perceived value of just about anything
claims.hypothesis: Among listings for physically identical goods, how upmarket the listing reads predicts the asking price, after allowing for seller and platform.
claims.rival: A list of luxury words; an LLM asked to score how upmarket each listing reads; sentence embeddings.
claims.data: Marketplace listings of unbranded goods sold under several brand names. Source and licence to confirm.

claims.claim: Renaming a product into a new category (toaster oven to air fryer, cake to muffin) raises its price and makes buyers happier with it.
claims.quote: re-branding a toaster oven as an ‘air fryer’ lets you increase the price, and customers are happier with their purchase
claims.hypothesis: Products with matching specifications sell at a higher price and get higher review scores under the newer category name than under the older one.
claims.rival: No content measure is involved: the category name and a table of specifications.
claims.data: Retail listings with specifications, prices and review scores for air fryers and convection ovens.

claims.claim: A good story must carry a non-obvious truth: it overturns a default expectation, such as that evil is strong, ugly is bad or fast wins.
claims.quote: It stands to reason that a good story needs to contain a non-obvious truth.
claims.hypothesis: Stories that last pair a trait with the opposite of its usual outcome (the weak win, the ugly are good) more often than forgotten stories of the same period and genre.
claims.rival: An LLM asked which common expectation the story overturns; a rare-pairing score built on words, as in RX-23.
claims.data: Folktales with counts of how widely each spread, or film plots with ratings. Usual pairings estimated from the 1,000 random film plots in preregistration/sources.

claims.claim: Any popular story can be reduced to a semiotic square: two opposed concepts and a contradiction between them.
claims.quote: You can break down any popular story with this framework
claims.hypothesis: Independent readers, human or LLM, given the same popular story name the same pair of opposed concepts far more often than chance.
claims.rival: Agreement between two LLM readers is the whole test. Neuron units would only confirm that both poles are present in the text.
claims.data: About 200 well-known film or folktale plots, each read by several independent readers.

claims.claim: Successful campaigns reuse the truth of a known fable: Guinness retells the Tortoise and the Hare, Dove retells Beauty and the Beast.
claims.quote: It’s a modern day Tortoise and Hare story, but this time carrying a valuable brand association.
claims.hypothesis: With names and shared words removed, a campaign's description is closer in neuron units to the fable it is paired with than to decoy fables, where word overlap cannot make the link.
claims.rival: Sentence embeddings; an LLM asked which fable each campaign echoes, which may well win.
claims.data: The essay's three pairs are only a pilot. A larger set needs campaign descriptions paired with fables by blind human judges. CJ-S7 is a similar test on film families.

claims.claim: Shared stories shape behaviour: without hero, rags-to-riches and Icarus stories there would be fewer heroic deeds, less upward mobility and more falls from grace.
claims.quote: Imagine a society where these stories didn’t exist. We’d have fewer heroic deeds, lower upwards social mobility, and more falls from grace.
claims.hypothesis: Societies whose recorded folklore holds more rags-to-riches tales show higher measured social mobility, or stronger belief in it, after allowing for region and income.
claims.rival: Existing human-coded motif catalogues of folklore. Counting their tags is enough.
claims.data: A cross-cultural folklore motif catalogue joined to survey and mobility data. Sources to confirm. The result would be a correlation, not proof of cause.

claims.claim: Precision costs exponentially more, so use only as much as the decision needs.
claims.quote: precision comes at a cost, and it increases exponentially
claims.hypothesis: For detecting memes in text, each further gain in accuracy costs a multiple of the last: word counts get most of the way, and neuron units buy the final few points at many times the compute.
claims.rival: Word counts, sentence embeddings and an LLM reader, all placed on one chart of cost against accuracy.
claims.data: The head-to-head results US-01 already plans to collect, with compute cost per story recorded for each method.

claims.claim: Breaking an estimate into parts and multiplying rough guesses lands within a factor of ten, because the errors cancel.
claims.quote: Even though each estimate might be off, aggregating lots of smaller errors cancels them out.
claims.hypothesis: Forecasts of a work's audience built from separately guessed parts land within a factor of ten of the truth more often than one-shot guesses by the same estimator.
claims.rival: A one-shot guess from the same LLM or person. No content measure is involved.
claims.data: Films or books with known audience figures; estimates from LLMs or a paid panel. This is a claim about estimating, not about how ideas spread.

claims.claim: New technologies start by copying the old one's forms and shed them as users grow familiar.
claims.quote: As our familiarity increases, Skeuomorphism gives way to flat design, de-cluttering old memes and fully utilising the new medium.
claims.hypothesis: Writing about a new technology carries the neuron units of the technology it replaced most strongly at launch, and their share falls steadily as the new category ages.
claims.rival: Counts of the old category's words ('horseless carriage') over time; embedding similarity to text about the old category.
claims.data: Dated public text on several transitions (carriage to car, whiskey to vodka in US adverts, film to digital camera): newspaper archives, book n-grams, patents. H18 uses the same traits as lineage markers; this asks for the decay curve.

claims.claim: Carried-over design features help only people who knew the original technology.
claims.quote: Studies show that older generations prefer Skeuomorphic designs, but they provide no value to newer generations
claims.hypothesis: A reference to an older technology improves comprehension or preference only among people who used the original. For younger groups the effect is zero or negative.
claims.rival: No text measure is involved: a preference or comprehension test by age band.
claims.data: A new panel study by age band, or published usability studies that compare the two design styles by age.

claims.claim: When a job title's reputation is spoiled, the better practitioners take a new title for much the same work: marketer to growth hacker, business analyst to data scientist.
claims.quote: If your meme gets polluted, it’s time to rebrand with new memes.
claims.hypothesis: Job adverts under the new title describe nearly the same tasks as adverts under the old title a few years earlier, while the new title carries a pay premium that shrinks as it spreads.
claims.rival: Word-weight or embedding similarity of the advert text with the title removed; an LLM listing the tasks in each advert.
claims.data: Dated job adverts with title, description and pay. Dataset and licence to confirm. US-02 asks a related question about invented code words.

claims.claim: A new label signals quality only while it is costly to adopt and hard to fake.
claims.quote: This only works if the label is costly, and can’t be easily faked.
claims.hypothesis: Labels that cost something to adopt (an exam, a licence, a title that closes other doors) keep their pay or price premium longer than labels anyone can claim for free.
claims.rival: No content measure is involved: the premium over time, by kind of label.
claims.data: Pay by job title and by certification over time.

claims.claim: Giving a concept a name makes it easier to remember and pass on.
claims.quote: Naming a thing makes it easier remember, because it creates an anchor in our memory

essays.name: A rose by any other name

claims.hypothesis: A concept described in papers before it had a name spreads faster after a compact name is coined than its earlier trend predicts. Finding the concept before it had a name is the step keyword counts cannot do.
claims.rival: Sentence-embedding search, or an LLM reading passages for the concept. Keyword counts work only after the coinage.
claims.data: OpenAlex abstracts (CC0) around the coinage dates of well-documented terms. A dated list of coinages has to be built first.

claims.claim: A name brings its existing associations to whatever it is attached to: Project Lightspeed sounds fast, Project Tortoise slow.
claims.quote: If a name references a spot that’s already taken, its associations come with it.

essays.name: A rose by any other name

claims.hypothesis: An identical neutral description is rated differently (faster, safer, more fun) according to the name attached, in the direction of the name's earlier associations.
claims.rival: An LLM asked to rate the named project; human ratings of the name on its own.
claims.data: New: about 50 neutral descriptions crossed with names of known association, rated by a paid panel.

claims.claim: A person's name nudges their career: people called Dennis are over-represented among dentists.
claims.quote: people named Dennis are more likely to become Dentists

essays.name: A rose by any other name

claims.hypothesis: In public professional registers, people whose first name resembles the name of a profession are over-represented in it, after allowing for how common the name is by birth year and region.
claims.rival: No content measure is involved: name counts against a matched baseline. From memory, and unchecked here, the original finding has been disputed on these controls.
claims.data: Public licensing registers; census name frequencies by birth cohort.

claims.claim: Slang and jargon reveal which group a speaker belongs to.
claims.quote: Slang terms are commonly used between people who belong to the same social group – they tell you about the topic and the speaker.
claims.hypothesis: With the topic held fixed, a writer's community can be identified from their text, and jargon terms carry most of that signal.
claims.rival: Counts of words and letter sequences, the standard authorship method. It should win, since jargon is words.
claims.data: Posts on one topic from several online communities. Access to confirm. US-S1 asks the single-author version.

claims.claim: Lower-status people overuse jargon to sound more intelligent or important.
claims.quote: studies show that low-status people abuse it to sound more intelligent, important, or business-like
claims.hypothesis: Among authors writing on the same topic for the same venue, those of lower status (junior rank, lower-ranked institution) use more jargon per sentence than higher-status authors.
claims.rival: Jargon word lists, acronym counts and readability scores. No look inside a model is needed.
claims.data: OpenAlex abstracts with author seniority and institution, or dissertation titles by institution rank.

claims.claim: There is a best level of compression: too much jargon shuts readers out, too little wastes their time.
claims.quote: Compress too much and you exclude too many, elaborate too much and nobody will afford the time to ingest it.
claims.hypothesis: Uptake is an inverted U in jargon density. Within a field, moderately dense abstracts are cited most; denser abstracts gain citations inside the field and lose them from outside it.
claims.rival: The share of rare technical terms per sentence; readability scores.
claims.data: OpenAlex abstracts and citation links, split into citations from inside and outside the field.

claims.claim: Jargon is compression: 43 words of jargon carry what would take thousands of plain words.
claims.quote: compressing it to just 43 is useful work!
claims.hypothesis: A jargon passage and its plain-English expansion activate the same neuron units, so the jargon version carries more units per word. The match holds only in a model that knows the field.
claims.rival: Sentence embeddings of the two versions; an LLM asked whether they say the same thing. Word overlap should fail, since few words are shared.
claims.data: Technical abstracts paired with published plain-language summaries (a paired set to confirm), or LLM-written expansions checked by experts. IN-03 ran a rewording test at equal length.

claims.claim: Which message is shown matters more than who it is shown to. Personality-based targeting adds little; testing many messages does the work.
claims.quote: We’ve been focused on micro-targeting, when in reality creative testing was doing the heavy lifting.
claims.hypothesis: In experiments that cross several messages with several audience segments, the gap between the best and the average message is larger than the gain from matching each segment to its own best message. Falsified if matching gains are the larger of the two.
claims.rival: No content unit is needed. A variance split on message labels and segment labels settles it. A neuron reader adds something only if it can predict which message wins.
claims.data: Field experiments like those in the PNAS psychological-targeting paper the essay cites. Whether those data are open was not checked this session.

claims.claim: One position can be delivered through different appeals, each fitted to a personality type, such as group fun for extroverts and protection for anxious people.
claims.quote: You say the same thing but with two very different messages
claims.hypothesis: Pairs of ads that take the same position through different appeals share 'position' neuron units and differ on 'appeal' units. Units chosen on some topics separate position from appeal on unseen topics.
claims.rival: An LLM asked to name the position and the appeal of each ad; a probe trained on sentence embeddings; word lists for threat and for sociability.
claims.data: Built pairs: an LLM writer states one position with several assigned appeals across many topics. Real targeted ads from the essay's cited study if obtainable (not checked).

claims.claim: Slogans were tried out at small scale first, and the ones that got a response were then picked up by mass media. The Meme President repeats this.
claims.quote: tested first on social media, with those that resonated amplified by news media outlets hungry for controversy
claims.hypothesis: Message variants that win small early tests later become more common in mass media than variants that lost the same tests.
claims.rival: Exact-phrase counts find fixed slogans perfectly. Sentence embeddings cover reworded variants.
claims.data: Upworthy Research Archive: winners before a cut-off date, checked against headlines written after it.

claims.claim: An idea can persist because it comforts the person who holds it, whatever its record for society. Blaming a system is easier on the ego than blaming oneself.
claims.quote: Rather than take personal responsibility it’s softer on the ego to make it a political thing.
claims.hypothesis: Among versions of one story, the version that blames a system for a personal hardship draws more clicks or votes than the version that puts responsibility on the individual.
claims.rival: An LLM labelling each text as system-blame or self-blame would probably do. Word lists for blame are the floor.
claims.data: Upworthy Research Archive: randomised headline tests whose arms differ in who is blamed.

claims.claim: A political movement starts out tolerant and turns to suppressing rival ideas only later, once it is established.
claims.quote: It’s only later that the Communism meme agitates its hosts into neutralising rival memes, through censorship and police action against political deviants.
claims.hypothesis: In a movement's own dated writings, calls to silence rival views are rare while it is small and rise after it gains power, more than in matched movements that never gained power.
claims.rival: Keyword lists (traitor, censor, enemy of the people); an LLM reading each passage. Wording differs by era and movement, which is the only opening for neurons.
claims.data: A dated archive of one movement's periodicals covering its rise to power, plus a matched movement. None identified or checked this session.

claims.claim: Propaganda dehumanises the enemy so that people will fight. Military Memetics adds that it works by repeating xenophobic phrases that stress differences and hide similarities.
claims.quote: propaganda always seeks to dehumanise the enemy, so that soldiers are more willing to override their natural altruism
claims.hypothesis: A neuron unit chosen on some dehumanising metaphors (vermin) also fires on unseen ones (disease, machines). Its rate in one side's press about the other side rises before fighting starts.
claims.rival: Dehumanisation word lists; an LLM reading each passage; a probe on sentence embeddings.
claims.data: Dated newspaper archives from a country before and during a war. None identified or checked this session.

claims.claim: Institutions learn a lesson after each war and then forget it as the people who lived it leave and the manuals are rewritten.
claims.quote: only for those painful lessons to fade as veterans retire and regulations and manuals get updated
claims.hypothesis: Across successive editions of a doctrine manual, the share of text about morale and will to fight jumps in the first edition after a major war and declines in later editions.
claims.rival: Keyword counts (morale, will, spirit) or an LLM tagging paragraphs would do. Vocabulary shifts between eras are the only opening for neurons.
claims.data: Successive editions of U.S. Army operations manuals, which are government works. Availability as clean text was not checked.

claims.claim: Mocking an idea spreads it. Hostile coverage counts as exposure just as friendly coverage does.
claims.quote: His ideas were ridiculous, and as such were ridiculed, in the process: sharing them.
claims.hypothesis: A slogan's later adoption is predicted by its total mentions, hostile ones included, and hostile mentions add as much as friendly ones. Falsified if only friendly mentions predict later use.
claims.rival: Exact-phrase counts plus an LLM labelling each mention as mocking or endorsing. No neuron unit is needed for fixed slogans.
claims.data: MemeTracker phrase clusters (news and blogs, August 2008 to April 2009), with each mention labelled for stance.

claims.claim: Three-word slogans are a proven form that campaigns keep returning to.
claims.quote: Three word chants of the type Trump employed like “lock her up” and “build the wall” are a time-honoured tradition
claims.hypothesis: Three-word slogans are repeated in the press more often than shorter or longer slogans from the same campaigns, and winning campaigns use them more than losing ones.
claims.rival: A word count is the whole test. No content unit of any kind is needed.
claims.data: A list of campaign slogans by year and candidate, with press mention counts. No source was checked this session.

claims.claim: Message warfare favours outsiders: it can raise disorder but cannot build stability. A battle of wills says the same of insurgencies.
claims.quote: if the goal is to increase stability, it's the wrong tool for the job
claims.hypothesis: Within one randomised test, the message that attacks an institution wins over the message that defends or reassures. Challengers gain more from attack messages than incumbents do.
claims.rival: Sentiment word lists; an LLM labelling each message as attack or reassurance.
claims.data: Upworthy Research Archive for attack against reassurance. The challenger against incumbent part needs political ads with outcomes; none identified.

claims.claim: Troll accounts gained trust by addressing readers as members of their own group.
claims.quote: infiltrating groups using affirming identity-based language, for example “As Texans, we…”, “As veterans, we...”
claims.hypothesis: Posts that open by naming the reader's group draw more engagement than the same account's posts without it. One unit detects this address across groups it was not chosen on.
claims.rival: A pattern match for 'As X, we' and counts of 'we' and 'our' catch the literal cases. An LLM reader covers loose ones.
claims.data: The released Internet Research Agency Facebook ads and tweets, with impressions and clicks. Release terms were not checked this session.

claims.claim: Division is sown by amplifying grievances a group already holds and activating people already polarised. New grievances are not invented.
claims.quote: not by manufacturing reasons for each group to hate each other, but by emphasising real grievances expressed by each side
claims.hypothesis: Troll posts carry few ideas new to the target community: their units already appear in that community's earlier posts. The troll posts closest to earlier community content draw the most engagement.
claims.rival: Word overlap and sentence-embedding similarity between each troll post and the community's earlier posts.
claims.data: Internet Research Agency posts set against earlier genuine posts from the same communities. Neither corpus was checked this session.

claims.claim: One operator ran accounts on both sides of the same divides, and even staged opposing rallies.
claims.quote: They disseminated fake news both in support of, and against, divisive candidates like Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders.
claims.hypothesis: Accounts run by one operator on opposite sides share a signature that separates them from genuine partisans on both sides, once stance and topic are held fixed.
claims.rival: Function-word stylometry (counting small grammatical words); an embedding classifier; posting times and other metadata.
claims.data: Internet Research Agency tweets labelled by persona type, plus genuine partisan accounts from the same period. Not checked this session.

claims.claim: A warning given before a false claim arrives works better than a correction afterwards. Military Memetics makes the same bet on countering propaganda early.
claims.quote: you can innoculate them from disinformation ahead of time, much like a vaccine works on a virus
claims.hypothesis: A warning placed before a false claim cuts how often the claim is passed on in retellings more than the same correction placed after it.
claims.rival: An LLM judge or keyword match checking each retelling for the claim. No neuron unit is needed unless the claim survives in other words.
claims.data: Retelling chains, by LLM writers or people, seeded with a planted false claim and a warning placed before or after it.

claims.claim: Godwin's Law was a deliberately designed counter-meme, and it worked: it discredited Nazi comparisons in online argument.
claims.quote: its effect was to discredit anyone who calls someone else a Nazi to try to win an argument online
claims.hypothesis: After Godwin's Law became widely known, comments making a Nazi comparison scored lower and drew more rebuttals than matched comments in the same thread, and the comparison became rarer per thread.
claims.rival: A keyword list (Nazi, Hitler, fascist) finds nearly every case. An LLM reader covers oblique comparisons.
claims.data: Dated discussion archives with reply threads or scores, such as Usenet or Reddit. Access was not checked this session.

claims.claim: Repetition alone persuades (the 'mere exposure' effect). The Meme President says being talked about was enough.
claims.quote: simply showing your ad with more frequency is enough to convince people of its message. Familiarity breeds trust.
claims.hypothesis: A message unit's click effect rises with how often readers recently met the same idea. H25 (meme fatigue) predicts the opposite sign, so one test decides between the two.
claims.rival: Exact-phrase and word-frequency counts of recent exposure; sentence-embedding similarity to recent headlines.
claims.data: Upworthy Research Archive; Reddit resubmissions as used in ME-25.

claims.claim: Perceived quality follows from visible popularity, so buying a place on a ranking creates real demand.
claims.quote: Quality is a relative measure and largely perceived based on accolades that come from achieving quantity.
claims.hypothesis: Books that reached a bestseller list through bulk orders go on to sell more, or stay listed longer, than books of similar content that just missed the list.
claims.rival: No content unit is needed for the main test. Genre tags or sentence embeddings are enough to match books on content.
claims.data: Bestseller lists that flag bulk orders, plus later sales or weeks on the list. No source was checked this session.

claims.claim: Attention is a bottleneck, so a story can be killed by releasing many others at once, or by releasing it when nobody is looking.
claims.quote: all it takes to kill a story is to knock it out of the limelight
claims.hypothesis: A negative story about an actor fades from coverage faster in weeks when that actor is the source of many other stories, compared with matched stories that broke in quiet weeks.
claims.rival: Named-entity and keyword counts per day; topic models. No neuron unit is needed.
claims.data: A dated news corpus with sources, such as MemeTracker's nine months of news and blogs.

claims.claim: The first story to fill a gap keeps its hold even after it is shown to be false.
claims.quote: were quickly debunked, but the impression remained and the information gap filled
claims.hypothesis: After a story is debunked, its named form declines while its name-free form (a lone pilot saving the capital) keeps appearing in later texts without the correction.
claims.rival: Keyword search finds the named form. An LLM reader or sentence embeddings must be beaten on the name-free form.
claims.data: Dated posts and articles about one debunked story, with fact-check dates. No corpus identified this session.

claims.claim: Groups whose culture spread pro-war ideas best displaced or absorbed more peaceful groups, so pro-war ideas were selected for.
claims.quote: Tribes infected with the best mechanisms for disseminating “war memes” either killed off more peaceful viewpoints
claims.hypothesis: Societies whose recorded folklore carries more war-praising motifs show more recorded warfare or wider spread, after allowing for shared ancestry between related societies.
claims.rival: The motif catalogue is already tagged by people, so the tags alone can test it. Neurons are not needed.
claims.data: Berezkin's folklore motif catalogue (958 societies, used in Michalopoulos and Xue 2021) joined to ethnographic warfare records. The join was not checked.

claims.claim: In a campaign the message matters more than the money behind it.
claims.quote: It is hard to overstate the relative importance in campaigns of message over resources
claims.hypothesis: Across many ballot campaigns, the content of each side's printed arguments predicts the result beyond the spending ratio, and adds more than spending does.
claims.rival: Spending ratio alone as the floor; then word counts, sentence embeddings and an LLM rating each argument's appeal.
claims.data: Ballot-measure results with campaign spending and the printed for-and-against arguments. No source was checked this session.

claims.claim: The winning message was found by listening: it put into words what ordinary voters already thought, where earlier campaigns spoke only to a radical tenth.
claims.quote: all I really did was listen
claims.hypothesis: Among a campaign's tested messages, winners share more ideas with what the audience was already saying in its own words than losers do, even where no words are shared.
claims.rival: Word overlap and sentence-embedding similarity between each message and the audience's own earlier text.
claims.data: Campaign messages with test results, set against earlier open-text survey answers or public posts from the same electorate. None identified this session.

claims.claim: The Leave campaign and the Trump campaign drew on the same underlying ideas (lost control, distrust of elites), in different national vocabularies.
claims.quote: These are essentially the same prevailing forces that conspired to elect Trump to office in 2016.
claims.hypothesis: Leave and Trump campaign texts sit closer to each other in neuron-unit profile than either sits to its own opponent, once place, party and person names are removed.
claims.rival: Sentence embeddings; an LLM listing each campaign's themes; word-weight similarity (TF-IDF) after names are removed.
claims.data: Public speeches, leaflets and ads from both 2016 campaigns and their opponents. No corpus was checked this session.

claims.claim: A meme such as Batman has no agreed edge because it is built from smaller memes (orphan, playboy, vigilante), which are built from others in turn.
claims.hypothesis: The neurons that fire for Batman can be predicted from the neurons that fire for his component memes plus a small remainder, and the same breakdown holds across different texts.
claims.rival: An LLM's list of tags combined by simple set arithmetic; adding sentence embeddings together.

claims.claim: Each observer holds a slightly different version of a meme, so my Batman is not your Batman and no shared unit can be pointed to.
claims.hypothesis: The neurons that mark Batman differ between models; after mapping one model onto another, agreement stays below the agreement of one model with itself. If agreement is high, the objection fails for models.
claims.rival: Agreement between two embedding models' neighbour lists, or between two LLMs' tag lists, which may be just as high.

claims.claim: How a meme is held depends on how much its holder has been exposed to it, so well-known memes should be shared more exactly than obscure ones.
claims.hypothesis: Agreement between models on a meme rises with how often the meme appears in their training text; niche memes do not carry over from one model to another.
claims.rival: The same trend measured with embedding neighbour lists or LLM tag lists instead of neurons.

claims.claim: Dawkins's three traits decide which memes survive: how accurately they are copied (fidelity), how much they spread (fecundity) and how long they last (longevity).
claims.hypothesis: Memes whose neuron profile changes least from one retelling to the next last longer and spread further.
claims.rival: The same test using how much the wording varies between retellings.

claims.claim: Who shares a meme often matters more than what the meme is, so studying memes apart from their carriers is a mistake.
claims.hypothesis: In data on what spreads, the content of a message explains less of its success than the identity of whoever shared it.
claims.rival: Follower count or prestige alone; keywords as the content measure. No neurons needed to test the claim.

claims.claim: Memes no longer need human hosts: they now exist inside artificial neural networks.
claims.hypothesis: This is premise P1 stated as a conjecture. It holds if H1 (detection), H5 (steering) and H8 (agreement between models) all hold together.
claims.rival: The rivals of H1, H5 and H8: keywords, sentence embeddings, an LLM reading the text, and prompting in place of steering.

claims.claim: Good ideas are reinvented independently (pyramids, calculus, a Romeo and Juliet plot), so likeness between two works does not prove one copied the other.
claims.hypothesis: Incidental details that serve no purpose ('hitchhikers', Mike's term) are shared by true descendants and absent from look-alikes that arose independently.
claims.rival: Word-level hitchhikers: rare shared words and named details.

claims.claim: Copying a finished product (a tune learned by ear) and copying its instructions (reading the notes) are different routes, and the second should lose less.
claims.hypothesis: Retellings made from memory drift further in neuron readings than re-performances made from a script.
claims.rival: Drift in wording; an LLM coding which statements survive.

claims.claim: Two ideas or products that fill the same niche cannot both last: one dies out or moves to a different niche.
claims.quote: If two species occupy the same niche, one will inevitably drive the other to extinction.
claims.hypothesis: Among pairs of near-identical works or brands launched together, one loses audience or the pair grows apart over time, more than matched dissimilar pairs do. New entrants that start far from incumbents survive longer.
claims.rival: Genre tags, word overlap or sentence embeddings as the measure of 'same niche'. Any of them could run this test.
claims.data: Twin films (two studios, same premise, same year) with box office; rival brands' copy over years. Opposite prediction to CJ-S6 and RX-S3, which expect rivals to converge.

claims.claim: People take on the ideas of those they spend most time with, beyond what genes explain.
claims.quote: We inherit the memes of those around us: everything from language to culture and preferences.
claims.hypothesis: A person's later writing takes up the idea units of the people they were most exposed to, more than those of equally similar people they were not exposed to.
claims.rival: Word or phrase uptake from the same contacts; embedding similarity.
claims.data: An email archive or follower graph where exposure is recorded.

claims.claim: New trends start with outsiders who are not trying to be copied, are picked up by celebrities, and only then reach the general public.
claims.quote: So while the general population is busy imitating celebrities, the celebrities themselves are desperately looking for the next trend.
claims.hypothesis: A new idea unit appears first in low-status or fringe sources, next in high-status accounts, last in the mass. The reverse order (celebrities first) is rarer than chance.
claims.rival: First-use dates of keywords or hashtags by account size. An LLM tagging posts.
claims.data: Dated posts with follower counts; fashion or music press against subculture forums. H24 covers early warning from fringes but not the three-step order.

claims.claim: A thing keeps its identity even after every part has been replaced; identity lies in the whole, not in any one part.
claims.quote: what makes it a ship is not any one part but the concept as a whole
claims.hypothesis: In a long-running franchise, each work shares many units with its neighbours in time, yet the newest works share almost none with the first. No single unit is present in every work readers accept as the same character.
claims.rival: The same turnover count on content words, or on an LLM's trait list per work.
claims.data: The 32 studied Batman works from 1939 on, names removed; Sherlock Holmes or Robin Hood as a second case.

claims.claim: Because ideas are now recorded and shared digitally, good ones should rarely die out.
claims.quote: most of the best memes we create may never be forgotten
claims.hypothesis: The share of story units that vanish from new works per decade is lower after mass recording (home video, the web) than before, at equal starting frequency.
claims.rival: Extinction rates of words, phrases or genre tags over the same decades.
claims.data: A century of dated film plot summaries. Being stored is not the same as being reused, so the test is on reuse.

claims.claim: Most changes to an idea neither help nor harm it; they ride along with whatever carries them.
claims.quote: In memes as in genes, the great majority of mutations are thought to be selectively neutral
claims.hypothesis: For most units, change in frequency over time is no larger than random copying with occasional innovation predicts; only a small minority show selection.
claims.rival: The same neutral test run on words or tags.
claims.data: Eighty years of film plots.

claims.claim: An idea that helps or is harmless in one setting can become harmful when the setting changes.
claims.quote: Eventually reality changes, and a meme that was neutral or even beneficial, can suddenly put you at risk.
claims.hypothesis: A unit's link with success is not fixed: its effect measured before a dated shock (a war, a new medium, a scandal) changes sign or size afterwards more often than a shuffled-date control.
claims.rival: The same before-and-after test on keywords or topic tags.
claims.data: Archived randomised headline tests or box office split by era. FI-22 tests whether winners persist; this tests when they flip.

claims.claim: Generation labels such as Gen Z tell you little about behaviour, while the Big Five personality traits (extraversion, agreeableness, openness, conscientiousness, neuroticism) predict it reliably.
claims.quote: is about as useful as the Signs of the Zodiac
claims.hypothesis: With age and year held fixed, a writer's generation label cannot be predicted from their text better than chance, while their measured Big Five scores can.
claims.rival: Word-count personality models, which already predict traits from text; sentence embeddings.
claims.data: Public essays or posts with author birth year and personality questionnaire scores.

claims.claim: Stories that give human feelings to animals and objects are unusually popular, because human brains over-detect minds.
claims.quote: Anthropomorphism forms the basis of many of our most popular stories to this day
claims.hypothesis: Tales and films whose lead is a human-like animal or object spread to more cultures, or earn more, than matched stories with human leads.
claims.rival: A 'talking animal' genre tag, a keyword list, or an LLM reading the plot.
claims.data: Folktale index with spread by culture; animated films with budget and box office. CE-S1 tests a neighbouring idea (a few expectation-breaking elements).

claims.claim: A belief sticks better when the receiver works part of it out, which is why conspiracy groups hand out clues, not conclusions.
claims.quote: a belief is more likely to take hold if you partially had a hand in researching it
claims.hypothesis: With topic held fixed, messages that leave the conclusion for the reader to reach (clues, open questions, 'look into it') are shared and repeated more than messages that state it outright.
claims.rival: A pattern match for question marks and 'do your research'; an LLM rating how much is left unsaid.
claims.data: Randomised headline tests (curiosity-gap arms against plain arms); forum posts with reply and repost counts.

claims.claim: Unlike gene mutations, changes to ideas are aimed: people discard bad variants in their heads before trying them.
claims.quote: Bad ideas can quickly be ruled out and forgotten by an active imagination, before even wasting resources testing them in the real world.
claims.hypothesis: Changes made during adaptation are not random draws: units added by adapters are already associated with success more often than units picked at random from the pool. Change comes from transformation as well as selection.
claims.rival: The same split computed on words or tags.
claims.data: Documented book-to-film links.

claims.claim: Ideas improve faster when several people explain, challenge and edit them than when one person works alone.
claims.quote: it typically needs to be explained, challenged, and improved by multiple other brains before being put into practice
claims.hypothesis: At an equal number of rewrites, a text revised by several different editors reaches higher blind-rated quality, and changes more units per step, than one revised by a single editor.
claims.rival: Quality judged by an LLM; change measured by edit distance.
claims.data: Revision histories with editor counts (wiki articles, co-written scripts) or built chains with one or many LLM or human editors.

claims.claim: Following Jaynes: characters in the Iliad do not reflect on their own thoughts; gods prompt their actions. Introspection appeared in writing only about 3,000 years ago.
claims.quote: may not have developed until as recently as 3,000 years ago
claims.hypothesis: Units for a character reasoning about their own mind are rarer in the Iliad than in the Odyssey and later texts, and rise with date, while units for god-prompted action fall.
claims.rival: Counts of mental-state words. A word-based study of this reportedly exists [UNVERIFIED]. Translators' word choices are the confound for every method.
claims.data: Dated ancient texts in the original language and in two independent translations each.

claims.claim: Ideas that last a very long time must benefit the people who hold them; harmful ones kill their hosts or get dropped.
claims.quote: Nothing that conferred a disadvantage on its hosts could have persisted for so long.
claims.hypothesis: Among advice-type ideas with a known verdict (works, does nothing, harms), the ones that work stay in circulation longer than the ones that harm.
claims.rival: Human or LLM tags for each piece of advice. No model internals are needed.
claims.data: Dated proverbs, folk remedies or health claims paired with later evidence reviews or fact-check verdicts.

claims.claim: Idea bundles spread when they push holders to display them publicly and recruit others.
claims.quote: Religions spread by agitating their hosts to display these symbols, turning followers into brand ambassadors.
claims.hypothesis: Texts carrying a 'show this' or 'pass this on' instruction are copied more often than matched texts without one.
claims.rival: A phrase list for 'share', 'forward', 'wear'; an LLM judge.
claims.data: Chain letters and copy-pasted posts with copy counts.

claims.claim: Institutions shielded from competition stop adapting and decline; those exposed to competition change and grow stronger.
claims.quote: monopolistic religious institutions fail to innovate and eventually decline in relevance
claims.hypothesis: The messages of protected institutions (state churches, monopoly broadcasters) change fewer units per decade than those of competing ones, and slower change goes with later loss of audience.
claims.rival: Word-level drift per decade.
claims.data: Dated sermons or mission statements from state and free churches; public and commercial broadcasters, with membership or audience series.

claims.claim: How strongly a source holds an idea decides whether it is passed on: weakly religious parents rarely raise religious children.
claims.quote: with less intensely religious parents, children are shown to be far less likely to be religious when they grow up
claims.hypothesis: Along documented source-to-adaptation links, a unit's chance of being inherited rises with how strongly or how often the source expresses it.
claims.rival: How often the matching words occur in the source.
claims.data: Source and adaptation pairs with per-unit strength in the source. ME-S11 and PO-S2 are near neighbours but ask about citations and canon tier.

claims.claim: Once a habit or belief is dropped it rarely comes back.
claims.quote: When old habits are broken, they tend to stay that way.
claims.hypothesis: Within a documented lineage, a unit lost at one step is regained in later steps less often than a never-held unit of equal overall frequency is gained.
claims.rival: Loss and regain of keywords or tags along the same lineage.
claims.data: Franchise series and adaptation chains. This is the opposite prediction to CJ-25 (faded memes return after about thirty years).

claims.claim: An idea has no fixed worth; how well it does depends on which other ideas are common around it.
claims.quote: Memes have no objective value, separate from the surrounding culture
claims.hypothesis: A unit's effect on success depends on the current share of a named rival unit: it wins when the rival is rare and loses when the rival is common.
claims.rival: The same interaction test on keywords or topic tags.
claims.data: Randomised headline tests dated by week, with each unit's share in recent headlines. FI-S5 covers a unit's own share only.

claims.claim: The mix of opposing ideas is self-correcting: it swings after a shock, then returns to a stable balance.
claims.quote: Once an evolutionarily stable strategy is reached, the balance of power only gets disrupted by large technological or environmental shifts.
claims.hypothesis: The share of aggressive against conciliatory units in a long text series returns to a stable level after each excursion, and excursions follow dated shocks. A random walk fits worse.
claims.rival: Word-list counts of hawkish and dovish vocabulary.
claims.data: Decades of parliamentary speeches or newspaper editorials with dated wars and technology shifts.

claims.claim: There is a best rate of change: ideas that change too little cannot adapt, ideas that change too much waste what already works.
claims.quote: memes that change too much will waste resources exploring new avenues, instead of exploiting existing pathways that are working
claims.hypothesis: Series whose instalments change a moderate share of units from one to the next last longer and earn more than series that change very little or a great deal.
claims.rival: Change between instalments measured by word overlap or embeddings. H29 is about novelty against a category, not rate of change within a line.
claims.data: Film and television series with instalment dates, earnings and cancellation dates.

claims.claim: A new idea is rejected unless it hooks onto something the receiver already holds.
claims.quote: attach themselves to something a person already has in their brains
claims.hypothesis: A unit new to a genre spreads further when its first appearances sit alongside units already common there.
claims.rival: Co-occurrence of the new keyword with common keywords.
claims.data: First appearances of units in film genres and their later spread.

claims.claim: Idea bundles that last have a keeper, a person or institution that preserves them and prunes outdated parts.
claims.quote: any good memeplex that has lasted over time has been curated by a person or institution
claims.hypothesis: Stories with an owner controlling the canon drift less per retelling and keep their core units longer than stories with no keeper, at equal age and popularity.
claims.rival: Lexical drift between retellings.
claims.data: Owned characters against public-domain or folk characters; the same character before and after copyright expiry.

claims.claim: Emotion, above all fear of threats, decides which ideas are remembered and passed on.
claims.quote: So we needed to evolve a mechanism for deciding what to remember: emotion.
claims.hypothesis: In retelling chains, statements carrying threat or strong-emotion units survive more steps than neutral statements of equal length and position.
claims.rival: Emotion word lists; an LLM rating each statement's arousal.
claims.data: Human retelling chains with statement-level survival.

claims.claim: A single neuron, or a handful, responds to one idea however it is expressed (name, picture, description), which Mike calls close to a definition of a meme.
claims.hypothesis: A small set of neurons fires for a named meme across its name, a name-free description, a paraphrase and a translation, and stays quiet on matched control texts.
claims.rival: Keyword match for named forms; sentence embeddings and an LLM asked 'is this Batman?' for name-free forms.

claims.claim: If a meme's neuron also fires on some other work, the two are probably related, so shared neurons should reveal links nobody had noticed.
claims.hypothesis: Searching for works with the same active neurons returns related works that people or the written record confirm, more often than embedding search does, especially where the two texts share few words.
claims.rival: Nearest neighbours by sentence embedding; word search on the same texts.

claims.claim: A system that can recognise a meme can also produce it: classifying something is halfway to generating it.
claims.hypothesis: Turning a meme's neurons up or down while a model writes moves the text toward or away from that meme, as judged by blind human raters.
claims.rival: Adding or removing the meme's keywords in the prompt, or simply asking the model for the change.

claims.claim: A model that has seen every example of a category knows what belongs in it better than the people who made the examples.
claims.hypothesis: Where a model's neurons draw the edge of a category predicts human category judgements better than a written definition or a tag list does.
claims.rival: An LLM classifying from a written definition with no examples; keyword lists; a simple classifier on sentence embeddings.

claims.claim: Some 'magic words' lift ad results in every account, and can be found by tying word sequences to performance.
claims.hypothesis: Neuron features that predict results in one account carry over to another account better than word sequences (n-grams) do.
claims.rival: Mike's own n-gram method: word sequences tied to performance.

sources.title: Comparative phylogenetic analyses uncover the ancient roots of Indo-European folktales
sources.used_for: The one quantitative study the essays lean on: proof that story traits can be traced "back to the Bronze age" without a formal unit, and an example of long-lived memes.
sources.finding: Across Indo-European peoples, which magic tales a population tells follows language ancestry, not geographic closeness; one tale, 'The Smith and the Devil', is traced to the Bronze Age (da Silva and Tehrani 2016).
sources.replication_idea: Read tale-type presence from neuron units on tale texts in several languages, then rerun the ancestry-versus-geography test. Rival: the hand-coded folktale index table the paper used, and word overlap between translated texts. CJ-S3 uses these data but does not rerun this test.

sources.title: The emotional arcs of stories are dominated by six basic shapes
sources.used_for: Evidence that only a few story shapes exist: "found 6 core 'shapes'", offered beside Booker's seven plots as support for a finite number of viable stories.
sources.finding: Scoring words for happiness along 1,327 Project Gutenberg fiction texts (1,737 in the preprint Mike cites) yields six basic emotional arcs; some arcs go with more downloads (Reagan et al. 2016).
sources.replication_idea: Rebuild the arcs from emotion units read along each text and test whether six arcs reappear and predict downloads. Rival: the original word-happiness list, which is already a word count, so neurons must add something beyond it.

sources.title: What Makes online Content Viral?
sources.used_for: Support for the advice that stories invoking "fear, anger, disgust, or sadness" are most shared. The paper does not say this; see folk_facts.
sources.finding: Among three months of New York Times articles, positive pieces were emailed more than negative ones; high-arousal emotions (awe, anger, anxiety) raised sharing and sadness lowered it (Berger and Milkman 2012).
sources.replication_idea: Fix units for awe, anger, anxiety and sadness in advance, then test on archived randomised headline tests whether arousal units win and sadness units lose. Rival: emotion word lists (the paper's own method) and an LLM rating each headline's emotion.

sources.title: Longitudinal analysis of sentiment and emotion in news media headlines using automated labelling with Transformer language models
sources.used_for: Evidence that news headlines have grown more negative since 2000, read as outlets chasing what gets shared.
sources.finding: In 23 million headlines from 47 US outlets, 2000 to 2019, headlines denoting anger rose 104%, fear 150%, disgust 29%, sadness 54%, and neutral ones fell 30% (Rozado, Hughes and Halberstadt 2022).
sources.replication_idea: Re-measure the trend with fixed emotion units on a public headline sample, and test whether units that win randomised click tests are the ones that became common. Rival: a sentiment word list and the paper's fine-tuned classifier.

sources.title: Phylomemetics—Evolutionary Analysis beyond the Gene
sources.used_for: Source of the word 'phylomemetics' and of the case for borrowing family-tree methods from biology to study culture.
sources.finding: Review: scribes' copying errors let standard tree-building programs rebuild a manuscript's copying history; the same methods are used on languages and artefacts, with networks where borrowing occurs (Howe and Windram 2011).
sources.replication_idea: On hand-copied manuscript traditions with a known tree, test whether neuron memes at least tie string-based methods at recovering it. Rival: variant-reading and string-distance methods used in manuscript studies.

sources.title: Phylomemetic Patterns in Science Evolution—The Rise and Fall of Scientific Fields
sources.used_for: Listed as an example of lineages of ideas rebuilt automatically from text.
sources.finding: Clusters of co-occurring terms, linked year to year, form lineages of science fields; a field's density correlates with its age and short-term survival (Chavalarias and Cointet 2013).
sources.replication_idea: Rebuild field lineages from neuron units on abstracts and test whether unit-based density forecasts which fields survive better than term density does. Rival: the paper's own term co-occurrence method. Extends ME-21's citation corpus.

sources.title: On the Origins of Memes by Means of Fringe Web Communities
sources.used_for: Background for the claim that memes differ in how fast they spread, burn out and mutate.
sources.finding: Grouping 160 million images by perceptual hash (a fingerprint of near-identical pictures), 4chan's /pol/ produced the most memes and The_Donald was best at pushing them into mainstream communities (Zannettou et al. 2018).
sources.replication_idea: Regroup image-meme variants by vision-model neurons and test whether the who-influences-whom estimates change once redrawn variants are joined. Rival: perceptual hash (the paper's method) and image embeddings. ME-S1 uses the same Know Your Meme labels.

sources.title: Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks
sources.used_for: The 2022 root of the neuron idea: such neurons are "a near definition of a meme"; the Spider-Man neuron is the example.
sources.finding: Single neurons in the CLIP image-text model respond to one concept whether it appears as a photo, a drawing or written text (Goh et al. 2021).
sources.replication_idea: Test whether a unit chosen on a scene described in words fires on the same scene as an image with no lettering. Rival: image-text embedding similarity and reading any words in the picture.

sources.title: Single-Cell Recognition: A Halle Berry Brain Cell
sources.used_for: Evidence that one brain cell fires for a person across photo, costume and written name, and that "different participants had different neural structures".
sources.finding: Press release on Quiroga et al. 2005 (Nature, doi 10.1038/nature03687, confirmed): single human brain cells respond to one person or landmark across very different pictures and the written name.
sources.replication_idea: Test whether a character unit fires on aliases and name-free descriptions and stays silent on the same word in another sense. Rival: keyword match for names; sentence embeddings for name-free forms.

sources.title: The Selfish Gene
sources.used_for: Definition of a meme as a unit copied by imitation; the three replicator traits (fidelity, fecundity, longevity); the hawk, dove and retaliator game.
sources.finding: Theory, no data: replicators that copy accurately, copy often and last long come to dominate, and ideas can be such replicators. [Existence checked in Open Library: Dawkins, 1976.]
sources.replication_idea: Test whether tale types whose tellings vary least in unit profile occur in more populations and reconstruct as older. Rival: the same test with word-level variation between tellings.

sources.title: The Meme Machine, Blackmore
sources.used_for: Source of 'memeplex' (memes that survive only together) and of the split between copying a product and copying its instructions.
sources.finding: Theory, no data: memes travel in mutually supporting bundles, and copying instructions drifts less than copying the finished product. [Existence checked in Open Library: Blackmore, 1999.]
sources.replication_idea: Along documented adaptation links, test whether bundle members are kept or dropped together beyond everyday co-occurrence; separately compare outline-based and text-based retelling chains (ME-S8, CE-S6). Rival: word co-occurrence and topic models.

sources.title: Meme Theory Oversimplifies Cultural Change
sources.used_for: Cited for the line that cultural-evolution scholars "criticised Memetics for oversimplification"; the essay does not engage the argument.
sources.finding: Boyd and Richerson (Scientific American, October 2000): "Memes are often systematically transformed during transmission", a process unlike natural selection; example, the ending '-gate' read differently by generations.
sources.replication_idea: In retelling chains, test whether new content is a copying error passed on, or something each chain adds independently. Rival: the same split measured with content words and with an LLM listing story elements.

sources.title: Cultural Macroevolution on Neighbor Graphs
sources.used_for: Listed among family-tree methods for culture; its warning about borrowing is not discussed.
sources.finding: For most of 44 cultural traits in 172 Western North American Indian societies, models using both language relatives and spatial neighbours fit best; trees alone lose information (Towner et al. 2012).
sources.replication_idea: For each film unit, fit presence with both documented-source neighbours and same-year, same-genre neighbours, and ask which carries more. Rival: the same model on word-count traits. PO-22 tests borrowing; LI-S3 audits tree-likeness.

sources.title: Phylogenetics and Material Cultural Evolution
sources.used_for: Listed behind the claim that technology lineages were "successfully reconstructed". The paper is a caution; see folk_facts.
sources.finding: For two musical instruments (psaltery, cornet), conventional tree methods do not give a general way to rebuild history, because designs transfer and blend in ways biology does not (Tëmkin and Eldredge 2007).
sources.replication_idea: On retellings built by merging two earlier versions, test whether neuron memes detect the second parent a tree would hide. Rival: word overlap with each candidate parent.

sources.title: Why Did Memetics Fail? Comparative Case Study
sources.used_for: Mike's whole account of why memetics stalled: it argued about what a meme is while rival researchers tested hypotheses; source of the '41 articles' count.
sources.finding: Historical case study: insisting on discrete units and separate memetic fitness pushed memeticists into defining units; gene-culture researchers tested hypotheses and attracted more scientists (Chvaja 2020).
sources.replication_idea: No neurons needed. Recount articles using 'memetics' by year in an open bibliographic database to check the 41 figure. For the programme: a warning against resting everything on the unit.

sources.title: The growth, spread, and mutation of internet phenomena: A study of memes
sources.used_for: Background for "different memes have always had different virality factors, retention rates and tendencies to mutate".
sources.finding: Fits epidemic-style (susceptible, infected, recovered) equations with random noise to the rise and fall of internet memes (Lonnberg, Xiao and Wolfinger 2020; abstract only read).
sources.replication_idea: Fit the same curves to neuron-unit frequencies by year in film plots and ask whether any unit departs from random copying. Rival: keyword and search-interest counts fitted the same way.

sources.title: When twice is better than once: increased liking of repeated items influences memory in younger and older adults
sources.used_for: Support for "mere exposure": showing an ad more often is "enough to convince people of its message". The paper tests liking, not belief; see folk_facts.
sources.finding: Repeated nonsense words and unfamiliar faces were liked more when repeats were spaced than back to back; older adults remembered liked items better (Palumbo et al. 2021).
sources.replication_idea: Mere exposure predicts repeats help; Mike's 'meme fatigue' predicts they hurt. When an image is reposted under a new title, test whether repeating an earlier title's idea in new words gains or costs votes. Rival: word overlap with earlier titles.

sources.title: Psychological targeting as an effective approach to digital mass persuasion
sources.used_for: Cited as evidence that personality targeting has a small effect, so that message testing, not targeting, did the work.
sources.finding: Three field experiments reaching over 3.5 million people: ads matched to extraversion or openness drew up to 40% more clicks and up to 50% more purchases (Matz et al. 2017).
sources.replication_idea: Plant an extravert-framed or introvert-framed meme in matched story premises and test whether readers' measured personality predicts which they prefer. Rival: an LLM asked which personality each text suits.

sources.title: Online Controlled Experiments at Large Scale
sources.used_for: Background for randomised tests as the standard of proof, and for the rule that big concept changes deserve tests while small variants ("1-2% differences") do not.
sources.finding: Bing ran over 200 concurrent experiments a day; the authors report a high rate of false positives and interactions between experiments that must be guarded against (Kohavi et al. 2013).
sources.replication_idea: Test whether the unit distance between two headline arms predicts the size of their click gap, so bigger creative changes give bigger differences. Rival: human tags and embedding distance between arms.

sources.title:
The Dilution Model: How Additional Goals Undermine the Perceived
Instrumentality of a Shared Path
sources.used_for: Support for 'say one thing': the more messages an ad carries, the less each lands. The paper did not test ads; see folk_facts.
sources.finding: Six experiments: the more goals one means serves (exercise for muscle and for weight loss), the less effective people judge it for each goal (Zhang, Fishbach and Kruglanski 2007).
sources.replication_idea: New. In randomised headline tests, count distinct meme units per arm and test whether the arm carrying more loses clicks, length held fixed. Rival: word count, and an LLM counting the claims in each headline.

sources.title: Ideas expressed with longer written descriptions are perceived as more creative than shorter ones
sources.used_for: One of a list of 'perception is leaky' effects: presentation changes how good an idea seems.
sources.finding: As reported in a social post: longer idea descriptions are rated more creative. The underlying paper could not be identified this session.
sources.replication_idea: No neurons needed for the claim, but it threatens every rating-based test here: measure how much of a unit's reading and of human ratings is explained by text length alone. Rival: plain word count.

sources.title: Skeuomorphs, Pottery, and Technological Change
sources.used_for: Evidence that features of an old technology are carried into its replacement, such as pottery shaped like woven baskets.
sources.finding: Review: skeuomorphs (features copied into a new material where they no longer do a job) help people accept an innovation by carrying over familiar value (Blitz 2015).
sources.replication_idea: Functionless carried-over details are markers of descent. Test whether incidental details shared by two films separate remakes from look-alike films with no documented link. Rival: rare shared words and named details.

sources.title: The Seven Basic Plots
sources.used_for: The claim that every successful story fits one of seven categories, so originality is recombination.
sources.finding: Booker's 2004 book sorts stories into seven plots by argument and example; it reports no counts or tests. [Existence checked on Wikipedia.]
sources.replication_idea: As films are added, test whether the number of distinct plot-level unit clusters levels off, and whether seven clusters fit better than five or twenty. Rival: clusters of sentence embeddings and LLM-assigned plot labels.

sources.title: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
sources.used_for: The Hero's Journey as the shared template behind Star Wars, Harry Potter, The Matrix and others.
sources.finding: Campbell's comparative mythology: hero myths worldwide share one sequence of stages, argued from examples, not measured. [Existence checked on Wikipedia.]
sources.replication_idea: Test whether units for the journey's stages appear in the claimed order in films said to follow it and not in matched decoys, shared vocabulary banned. Rival: an LLM labelling stages from the text.

sources.title: The Tipping Point: How Little Things Can Make a Big Difference
sources.used_for: 'Market mavens' and the tipping point: a few connected people carry an idea from innovators to everyone.
sources.finding: Popular account, not a study: spread depends on a few special carriers, on the message's 'stickiness' and on context. [Existence checked in Open Library: Gladwell, 2000.]
sources.replication_idea: With content held fixed, measure how much of a post's success its content explains against who posted it, where and when. Neurons are needed only for the content side. Rival: follower count alone; word features for content.

sources.title: Diffusion of Innovations Theory
sources.used_for: The S-curve of adoption and the adopter groups from innovators to laggards.
sources.finding: An explainer page on Rogers's theory that adoption follows an S-curve through five adopter groups. The page could not be fetched this session.
sources.replication_idea: When a unit first appears in a film genre, test whether its later spread beats random copying and whether spreaders can be picked from early data. Rival: keyword counts fitted the same way.

sources.title: Using Semiotics in Marketing: How to Achieve Consumer Insight for Brand Growth and Profits
sources.used_for: Semiotic 'codes' shared across a product category (UK toilet roll brands all show a baby or animal), the Charmin rebrand, and the semiotic square.
sources.finding: Practitioner method: categories share recurring signs that buyers expect, and analysts can list them by reading packs and ads. [Existence checked in Open Library: Lawes, 2020.]
sources.replication_idea: Test whether units shared by every brand in a category exist, and whether unit distance separates same-brand from rival-brand copy better than word overlap. Rival: a human analyst's tag list; TF-IDF.

sources.title: Wanting: Mimetic Desire: How to Avoid Chasing Things You Don't Truly Want
sources.used_for: Girard's theory that people copy the desires of models, so who shares an idea matters as much as the idea.
sources.finding: Popular account of Girard: desire is copied from models, and rivals grow alike. No tests reported. [Existence checked in Open Library: Burgis, 2021.]
sources.replication_idea: When a researcher meets an idea new to them, test whether adoption is explained more by which idea it is or by who displayed it. Rival: author prominence alone; word-based idea matching.

sources.title: Innovation as Evolution: Case Study Phylomemetic of Cellphone Designs
sources.used_for: Example of a technology treated as a species with traits whose evolutionary path was rebuilt.
sources.finding: Trees built from hand-coded cellphone features showed "a generally different branching pattern" from the tree given by model numbers and release dates (Khanafiah and Situngkir 2004).
sources.replication_idea: On product descriptions with a known release lineage, test whether unit-based trees match it better than the paper's hand-coded features did. Rival: word-count trees and LLM-listed features.

sources.title: Memes, genes, and signs: Semiotics in the conceptual interface of evolutionary biology and memetics
sources.used_for: The semiotic critique that a meme is a sign reduced to its ability to be copied.
sources.finding: Theory: proposes the sign (a thing standing for another thing) as the common concept behind gene and meme, to rebuild memetics on semiotics (Fomin 2019).
sources.replication_idea: A sign's meaning depends on who reads it. Test whether units separate euphemistic from literal uses of one phrase, which keyword counts cannot do. Rival: sentence embeddings and an LLM reading the passage.

sources.title: The Evolving Definition of the Term “Gene”
sources.used_for: Defence of memetics: the gene too began as an abstract unit and is still hard to define.
sources.finding: History: 'gene' moved from an abstract unit of inheritance to a DNA segment coding one protein chain; later findings made that definition obsolete (Portin and Wilkins 2017).
sources.replication_idea: Ask the same of memes: at what unit size (one neuron, merged family, sentence, document) does heredity along citations peak? Rival: the same curve for words and word clusters.

sources.title: Save the Cat!: The Only Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need: The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need
sources.used_for: Quoted for the claim that every film falls into a category with rules.
sources.finding: Screenwriting manual: films belong to a few genres, each with required beats at set points. Advice, not data. [Existence checked in Open Library: Snyder, 2005.]
sources.replication_idea: New. Test whether units for the book's named beats fire at the prescribed points in film synopses, and whether conforming films earn more. Rival: an LLM marking the beats; position in text alone.

sources.title: On the Origin of Stories: Evolution, Cognition, and Fiction
sources.used_for: The claim that storytelling was "our fundamental evolutionary survival trait".
sources.finding: Theory: fiction is an evolved form of cognitive play that holds attention with social and survival content (Boyd; Crossref lists Harvard University Press, 2009).
sources.replication_idea: When people retell a story, test whether fixed units predict which statements survive, and whether social and survival content survives best. Rival: content words and an LLM coding each statement.

sources.title: Neural correlates of maintaining one’s political beliefs in the face of counterevidence
sources.used_for: Support for the claim that disconfirming evidence makes people "believe it more". The paper found the opposite direction; see folk_facts.
sources.finding: Forty liberals shown counter-arguments lowered belief in both political and non-political statements, political ones least; resistance went with activity in emotion-related brain areas (Kaplan, Gimbel and Harris 2016).
sources.replication_idea: Weak fit for neurons. In retelling chains with a counter-argument inserted, test whether identity-linked claims survive more often than neutral ones. Rival: an LLM checking whether each claim is still present.

sources.title: Asymmetry in Belief Revision
sources.used_for: Quoted in the argument for forewarning people against misinformation before they meet it.
sources.finding: Three studies: people more easily come to believe a claim once thought false than stop believing one once thought true (Yang, Stone and Marsh 2022).
sources.replication_idea: Across outlets and years, test whether a retracted claim keeps appearing longer than a newly confirmed claim takes to spread. Rival: word counts and an embedding probe for the claim.

sources.title: Tra i Leoni: Revealing the Preferences Behind a Superstition
sources.used_for: Worked example that a rumour persists by conformity: students avoid walking between two lion statues because others do.
sources.finding: Field interventions and priced choices show both real belief and conformity sustain a university superstition; for many, adherence depends on what others do (Invernizzi et al. 2019).
sources.replication_idea: No neurons needed for the claim. Along citation links, test whether an idea's uptake depends on how many sources carry it or on which idea it is. Rival: word-based idea matching.

sources.title: Religion, fertility and genes: a dual inheritance model
sources.used_for: Background for the claim that religions persist through upbringing and larger families.
sources.finding: Model, not data: if religious people have more children, a gene predisposing to religion spreads even with many defections, by 'cultural hitch-hiking' on a high-fertility practice (Rowthorn 2011).
sources.replication_idea: Look for hitch-hiking among memes: after a hit film, test whether its optional units rise in later films and drag linked passenger units with them. Rival: the same test on word clusters.

sources.title: Crossing the Chasm, 3rd Edition: Marketing and Selling Disruptive Products to Mainstream Customers (Collins Business Essentials)
sources.used_for: The 'chasm' between early adopters and the early majority, which the essay credits to the wrong author; see folk_facts.
sources.finding: Practitioner claim: most new products stall between early adopters and the mainstream. [Existence checked in Open Library and Crossref: Geoffrey A. Moore, 1991.]
sources.replication_idea: Among units that first appear in a film genre, test for two outcomes with a gap between them (stall at a small share, or cross into most films). Rival: keyword counts.

sources.title: Differentiate or Die
sources.used_for: Title and thesis of the essay: two brands in one niche cannot coexist, so they must differ or one dies.
sources.finding: Practitioner claim, not data: brands that fail to differ lose to competitors. [Existence checked in Open Library: Trout, 2000.]
sources.replication_idea: Test whether the distance between competing firms' self-descriptions shrinks year on year, and whether firms that stay distinct survive longer. Rival: TF-IDF distance and Mike's tag-count distance.

sources.title: Rebranding Charmin: A case study in semiotics
sources.used_for: Natural experiment: renaming Charmin as Cushelle with a koala in the UK lost no sales; folding it into Zewa in Germany lost about a fifth.
sources.finding: Consultancy case study by the people who did the work: UK rebrand reported as a success; in Germany combined Charmin and Zewa brand share fell 21% (Lawes and Blackburne 2011).
sources.replication_idea: Two cases only. Test whether a brand score ranks Cushelle copy nearer to Charmin than Zewa copy, and keep it robust to pasted trigger words. Rival: word overlap, and an LLM asked which rebrand is closer.
